In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah Yasin. It is Meccan by unanimous consensus. It has eighty-three verses, except that a group said that His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And We record what they have sent before and their traces﴾ [Yasin: 12] was revealed concerning the Banu Salima of the Ansar when they wanted to leave their dwellings and move near the Mosque of the Messenger (ﷺ), as will come. In the Sunan of Abu Dawud, on the authority of Ma'qil ibn Yasar, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Recite Yasin over your dead." Al-Ajurri mentioned, from the hadith of Umm al-Darda' [[So it is in all the copies of the original; what is in al-Durr al-Manthur is Abi al-Darda'.]], on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "There is no dead person over whom Surah Yasin is recited except that Allah lightens it for him." In the Musnad of al-Darimi, on the authority of Abu Hurairah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Surah Yasin in a night seeking the Face of Allah, he will be forgiven in that night." Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz also related it. Al-Tirmidhi related, on the authority of Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Yasin. Whoever recites Yasin, Allah records for him by its recitation the reward of reading the Qur'an ten times." He said: This is a gharib hadith, and in its chain is Harun Abu Muhammad, an unknown shaykh. And concerning this chapter there is also a report from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, but the hadith of Abu Bakr is not sound in terms of its chain, and its chain is weak. And on the authority of Aisha that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed in the Qur'an there is a surah that intercedes for its reciters and whose listeners are forgiven. Behold, it is Surah Yasin, and it is called in the Torah al-Mu'imma." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is al-Mu'imma?" He said: "It encompasses its companion with the good of this world and repels from him the terrors of the Hereafter, and it is called al-Dafi'a and al-Qadiya." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, how is that?" He said: "It repels from its companion every evil and fulfils for him every need. Whoever recites it, it counts for him as twenty pilgrimages; whoever hears it, it is for him like a thousand dinars given in charity in the way of Allah; and whoever writes it and drinks it, it enters his belly as a thousand cures, a thousand lights, a thousand certainties, a thousand mercies, a thousand compassions, a thousand guidances, and removes from him every disease and rancor." Al-Tha'labi mentioned it from the hadith of Aisha, and al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim in Nawadir al-Usul mentioned it from the hadith of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, as a musnad report. In the Musnad of al-Darimi, on the authority of Shahr ibn Hawshab, who said: Ibn Abbas said: "Whoever recites Yasin in the morning is given the ease of his day until evening, and whoever recites it at the beginning of his night is given the ease of his night until morning." Al-Nahhas mentioned, on the authority of Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, who said: "For everything there is a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Yasin. Whoever recites it by day, his concern is relieved, and whoever recites it by night, his sin is forgiven." Shahr ibn Hawshab said: The people of Paradise recite only Ta-Ha and Yasin. Al-Mawardi raised these three reports to the Prophet, saying: Al-Dahhak related on the authority of Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Yasin. Whoever recites it in a night is given the ease of that night, and whoever recites it in a day is given the ease of that day. Indeed the people of Paradise will have the Qur'an lifted from them, so they will recite nothing but Ta-Ha and Yasin." Yahya ibn Abi Kathir said: "It has reached me that whoever recites Surah Yasin at night will remain in joy until morning, and whoever recites it in the morning will remain in joy until evening, and someone who tested it has related to me." Al-Tha'labi and Ibn Atiyya mentioned it. Ibn Atiyya said: Experience confirms this. Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim in Nawadir al-Usul mentioned, on the authority of Abd al-A'la, who said: Muhammad ibn al-Salt related to us from Umar ibn Thabit, from Muhammad ibn Marwan, from Abu Ja'far, who said: "Whoever finds hardness in his heart, let him write Yasin in a cup with saffron and then drink it." My father, may Allah have mercy on him, related to me, saying: Asram ibn Hawshab related to us, from Baqiyya ibn al-Walid, from al-Mu'tamir ibn Ashraf, from Muhammad ibn Ali, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Qur'an is better than everything apart from Allah, and the excellence of the Qur'an over other speech is like the excellence of Allah over His creation. Whoever honours the Qur'an has honoured Allah, and whoever does not honour the Qur'an has not honoured Allah. The sanctity of the Qur'an before Allah is like the sanctity of a father over his son. The Qur'an is an intercessor whose intercession is accepted, and an advocate whose testimony is believed. Whoever the Qur'an intercedes for, it is granted; whoever it argues against, it prevails over. Whoever makes it his leader, it leads him to Paradise; whoever makes it his follower, it drives him to the Fire." The bearers of the Qur'an are those surrounded by the sanctity of Allah, clothed in the light of Allah, taught the speech of Allah. Whoever befriends them has befriended Allah, and whoever opposes them has opposed Allah. Allah, Exalted is He, says: "O bearers of the Qur'an, respond to your Lord by honouring His Book, and He will increase you in love and make you beloved to His servants. The trials of this world are repelled from the listener of the Qur'an, and the trials of the Hereafter are repelled from its reciter. Whoever hears a verse from the Book of Allah, it is better for him than what is beneath the Throne down to the earth. Indeed in the Book of Allah there is a surah called al-Aziza, and its companion will be called al-Sharif on the Day of Resurrection; it will intercede for its companion for more than the tribes of Rabi'a and Mudar, and it is Surah Yasin." Al-Tha'labi mentioned, on the authority of Abu Hurairah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Surah Yasin on Friday night will wake up forgiven." And on the authority of Anas, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever enters the graveyards and recites Surah Yasin, Allah lightens the punishment for them that day, and he will have as many good deeds as the number of its letters."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Ya-Sin. By the wise Qur'an, indeed you are among the messengers, upon a straight path. A revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Ya-Sin﴾. Regarding "Yasin" there are several readings. The people of Medina and al-Kisa'i read "Yasin, wal-Qur'ani l-Hakim" with idgham of the nun into the waw. Abu Amr, al-A'mash and Hamza read "Yasin" with izhar of the nun. Isa ibn Umar read "Yasina" with a fatha on the nun. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Nasr ibn Asim read "Yasini" with a kasra. Harun al-A'war and Muhammad ibn al-Sumaiqa read "Yasinu" with a damma on the nun. These are five readings. The first reading, with idgham, is according to what is required in Arabic, because the nun is assimilated into the waw. Whoever makes it clear says the way of the letters of the alphabet (huruf al-hija') is to pause upon them, and idgham occurs only in continuous recitation (al-idraj). Sibawayh mentioned the fatha and gave it two aspects: one is that it is an object and is not declined, because it is for him a foreign noun like Habil, the implied sense being "Remember Yasina." Sibawayh made it the name of the surah. The other aspect is that it is indeclinable upon fatha, like kayfa and ayna. As for the kasra, al-Farra' claimed that it is made similar to the Arabic expression "jair, la af'alu" (by Allah, I will not do it), so on this view "Yasini" is an oath, and Ibn Abbas said so. It was also said: it is made similar to amsi, Hadhaam, ha'ulaa' and Raqash. As for the damma, it is made similar to mundhu, haythu and qatt, and to the vocative singular when you say "ya rajulu," for the one who pauses upon it. Ibn al-Sumaiqa and Harun said: It has been explained as "ya rajul," so the damma is the more fitting for it. Ibn al-Anbari said: "Yasin" is a good pause for those who say it is the opening of the surah; and for those who say the meaning of "Yasin" is "ya rajul," he does not pause upon it. It is related from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and others that its meaning is "ya insan" (O human being). They said of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Peace upon the family of Yasin﴾ [al-Saffat: 130], that it means "upon the family of Muhammad." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: It is one of the names of Muhammad (ﷺ), and its proof is "Indeed you are among the messengers." Al-Sayyid al-Himyari said:

O soul, do not exhaust yourself in sincere advice, striving,
and upon affection, except the family of Yasin.

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: Its meaning is "O master of mankind." It was also said: It is one of the names of Allah. Malik said, and Ashhab related from him: I asked him, "Is it fitting for anyone to name himself Yasin?" He said: "I do not think it is fitting, because of the words of Allah: 'Ya-Sin, wal-Qur'ani l-Hakim,' as if he says, 'This is My name, Yasin.'" Ibn al-‘Arabi said: This is a wonderful statement, for a servant may name himself with a name of the Lord if there is in it a meaning from Him, such as "knowing," "powerful," "willing," and "speaking." Malik only forbade naming with "Yasin" because it is one of the names of Allah whose meaning is not known, so perhaps its meaning is something exclusive to the Lord, and it is not permissible for the servant to presume upon it. If it is said: Allah, Exalted is He, has said: ﴿Peace upon the family of Yasin﴾ [al-Saffat: 130]. We say: That is written with its spelling (hijaʼ), so naming with it is permitted, and this which is not spelled out is what Malik spoke about, because of the difficulty in it, and Allah knows best. Some scholars said: Allah opened this surah with the letters ya and sin, and in them is the gathering of goodness. The opening indicates that it is a heart, and the heart is the ruler of the body; likewise "Ya-Sin" is the ruler over the rest of the surahs, encompassing the whole Qur'an. Then they differed about it as well. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ikrima said: It is in the language of Abyssinia. Al-Sha'bi said: It is in the language of Tayy. Al-Hasan: in the language of Kalb. Al-Kalbi: It is in Syriac, and the Arabs spoke it so it became part of their language. This meaning has already passed in [Ta-Ha] and in the introduction of the book, in full. Al-Qadi Iyad has laid out the views of the exegetes on the meaning of "Yasin." Abu Muhammad Makki related that it was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I have ten names with my Lord," and he mentioned that among them are Ta-Ha and Yasin, which are two of his names.

Qurtubi said: Al-Mawardi reported from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Allah the Exalted named me in the Qur'an with seven names: Muhammad, Ahmad, Ta-Ha, Ya-Sin, al-Muzzammil, al-Muddaththir, and Abdullah.'" Thus said al-Qadi. Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami related from Ja'far al-Sadiq that he meant "Ya Sayyid" (O master), addressing his Prophet (ﷺ). And from Ibn Abbas: "Ya-Sin" means "O man," meaning Muhammad (ﷺ). He also said: it is an oath, and it is one of the names of Allah the Glorified. Al-Zajjaj said: it has been said its meaning is "O Muhammad," and it has been said "O man," and it has been said "O human being." And from Ibn al-Hanafiyyah: "Ya-Sin" means "O Muhammad." And from Ka'b: "Ya-Sin" is an oath which Allah swore by before He created the heavens and the earth by two thousand years, [[An addition required by the context, and supported by what is related in al-Durr al-Manthur of al-Suyuti from Ka'b.]] "O Muhammad, indeed you are among the messengers" (ﷺ), then He said: "By the Wise Qur'an."

So if it is assumed that it is one of his names (ﷺ), and it is established that it is an oath, then there is in it the honour mentioned previously, and the oath is emphasised by the other oath being conjoined to it. And if it is in the sense of a call, then another oath has come after it, to confirm his messengership and to bear witness to his guidance. Allah the Exalted swore by His name and His Book: "Indeed you are among the messengers," through His revelation to His servants, "on a straight path," from His faith, meaning a path with no crookedness in it and no deviation from the truth.

Al-Naqqash said: Allah the Exalted did not swear for any of His prophets concerning messengership in His Book except for him, and in it is of his exaltation and glorification according to the interpretation of whoever says it means "O master," as is in it; and he (peace be upon him) said: "I am the master of the children of Adam." End of his words. Al-Qushayri related that Ibn Abbas said: The disbelievers of Quraysh said, "You are not a messenger, and Allah has not sent you to us," so Allah swore by the firm (muhkam) Qur'an that Muhammad is among the messengers. "Al-Hakim" means the made firm, so that it is not exposed to falsehood and contradiction, as He said: "Its verses have been made firm." Likewise it is made firm in its composition and its meanings, so no flaw reaches it. "Al-Hakim" in reference to Allah may mean "al-muhkim" with a kasra on the kaf, like "al-alim" meaning "al-mu'lim" (the one who causes pain). "On a straight path": that is, a straight religion, which is Islam. Al-Zajjaj said: on the way of the prophets who came before you. He said: "Indeed you are among the messengers" is the predicate of "inna," and "on a straight path" is a second predicate, meaning: indeed you are among the messengers, and indeed you are on a straight path. It has been said: the meaning is "among the messengers upon uprightness," so that his words "on a straight path" pertain to "the messengers," meaning: indeed you are among the messengers who were sent upon a straight manner, like His saying, Exalted is He: "And indeed you guide to a straight path, the path of Allah," that is, the path which Allah commanded.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful﴾. Ibn Amir, Hafs, al-A'mash, Yahya, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "tanzila" with a fatha on the lam, as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: Allah sent down that as a sending down. He made the verbal noun a construct, so it became definite, like His saying: ﴿So smiting of the necks﴾ [Muhammad: 4], meaning: smiting the necks. The rest read "tanzilu" with a damma, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is a revelation, or: what was sent down to you is the revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful. Also read: "tanzili" with a kasra, as a substitute (badal) for "al-Qur'an," and the revelation refers to the Qur'an. It has been said it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: indeed you are among the messengers, and indeed you are the revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful. So "tanzil" in this view means "sending" (irsal). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah has indeed sent down to you a reminder, a messenger reciting﴾ [al-Talaq: 10-11]. It is said: Allah sent the rain and sent it down, with the same meaning. Muhammad (ﷺ) is the mercy of Allah, which He sent down from the heaven. And whoever reads it with a fatha says: "Indeed you are among the messengers" by a sending from the Mighty, the Merciful. "Al-Aziz" means the one who takes vengeance upon whoever opposes Him, and "al-Rahim" means the one who is merciful toward the people of His obedience.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Al-Zajjaj said: it has been said its meaning is "O Muhammad," and it has been said "O man," and it has been said "O human being." And from Ibn al-Hanafiyyah: "Ya-Sin" means "O Muhammad." And from Ka'b: "Ya-Sin" is an oath which Allah swore by before He created the heavens and the earth by two thousand years, [[An addition required by the context, and supported by what is related in al-Durr al-Manthur of al-Suyuti from Ka'b.]] "O Muhammad, indeed you are among the messengers" (ﷺ), then He said: "By the Wise Qur'an."

Al-Naqqash said: Allah the Exalted did not swear for any of His prophets concerning messengership in His Book except for him, and in it is of his exaltation and glorification according to the interpretation of whoever says it means "O master," as is in it; and he (peace be upon him) said: "I am the master of the children of Adam." End of his words. Al-Qushayri related that Ibn Abbas said: The disbelievers of Quraysh said, "You are not a messenger, and Allah has not sent you to us," so Allah swore by the firm (muhkam) Qur'an that Muhammad is among the messengers. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

It has eighty-three verses, except that a group said that His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And We record what they have sent before and their traces﴾ [Yasin: 12] was revealed concerning the Banu Salima of the Ansar when they wanted to leave their dwellings and move near the Mosque of the Messenger (ﷺ), as will come. In the Sunan of Abu Dawud, on the authority of Ma'qil ibn Yasar, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Recite Yasin over your dead." Al-Ajurri mentioned, from the hadith of Umm al-Darda' [[So it is in all the copies of the original; what is in al-Durr al-Manthur is Abi al-Darda'.]], on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "There is no dead person over whom Surah Yasin is recited except that Allah lightens it for him." In the Musnad of al-Darimi, on the authority of Abu Hurairah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Surah Yasin in a night seeking the Face of Allah, he will be forgiven in that night." Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz also related it. Al-Tirmidhi related, on the authority of Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Yasin. Whoever recites Yasin, Allah records for him by its recitation the reward of reading the Qur'an ten times." He said: This is a gharib hadith, and in its chain is Harun Abu Muhammad, an unknown shaykh. And concerning this chapter there is also a report from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, but the hadith of Abu Bakr is not sound in terms of its chain, and its chain is weak. And on the authority of Aisha that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed in the Qur'an there is a surah that intercedes for its reciters and whose listeners are forgiven. Behold, it is Surah Yasin, and it is called in the Torah al-Mu'imma." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is al-Mu'imma?" He said: "It encompasses its companion with the good of this world and repels from him the terrors of the Hereafter, and it is called al-Dafi'a and al-Qadiya." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, how is that?" He said: "It repels from its companion every evil and fulfils for him every need. Whoever recites it, it counts for him as twenty pilgrimages; whoever hears it, it is for him like a thousand dinars given in charity in the way of Allah; and whoever writes it and drinks it, it enters his belly as a thousand cures, a thousand lights, a thousand certainties, a thousand mercies, a thousand compassions, a thousand guidances, and removes from him every disease and rancor." Al-Tha'labi mentioned it from the hadith of Aisha, and al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim in Nawadir al-Usul mentioned it from the hadith of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, as a musnad report. In the Musnad of al-Darimi, on the authority of Shahr ibn Hawshab, who said: Ibn Abbas said: "Whoever recites Yasin in the morning is given the ease of his day until evening, and whoever recites it at the beginning of his night is given the ease of his night until morning." Al-Nahhas mentioned, on the authority of Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, who said: "For everything there is a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Yasin. Whoever recites it by day, his concern is relieved, and whoever recites it by night, his sin is forgiven." Shahr ibn Hawshab said: The people of Paradise recite only Ta-Ha and Yasin. Al-Mawardi raised these three reports to the Prophet, saying: Al-Dahhak related on the authority of Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Yasin. Whoever recites it in a night is given the ease of that night, and whoever recites it in a day is given the ease of that day. Indeed the people of Paradise will have the Qur'an lifted from them, so they will recite nothing but Ta-Ha and Yasin." Yahya ibn Abi Kathir said: "It has reached me that whoever recites Surah Yasin at night will remain in joy until morning, and whoever recites it in the morning will remain in joy until evening, and someone who tested it has related to me." Al-Tha'labi and Ibn Atiyya mentioned it. Ibn Atiyya said: Experience confirms this. Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim in Nawadir al-Usul mentioned, on the authority of Abd al-A'la, who said: Muhammad ibn al-Salt related to us from Umar ibn Thabit, from Muhammad ibn Marwan, from Abu Ja'far, who said: "Whoever finds hardness in his heart, let him write Yasin in a cup with saffron and then drink it." Whoever honours the Qur'an has honoured Allah, and whoever does not honour the Qur'an has not honoured Allah. The sanctity of the Qur'an before Allah is like the sanctity of a father over his son. The Qur'an is an intercessor whose intercession is accepted, and an advocate whose testimony is believed. Whoever the Qur'an intercedes for, it is granted; whoever it argues against, it prevails over. Whoever makes it his leader, it leads him to Paradise; whoever makes it his follower, it drives him to the Fire." Whoever befriends them has befriended Allah, and whoever opposes them has opposed Allah. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Whoever makes it clear says the way of the letters of the alphabet (huruf al-hija') is to pause upon them, and idgham occurs only in continuous recitation (al-idraj). Sibawayh mentioned the fatha and gave it two aspects: one is that it is an object and is not declined, because it is for him a foreign noun like Habil, the implied sense being "Remember Yasina." Sibawayh made it the name of the surah. The other aspect is that it is indeclinable upon fatha, like kayfa and ayna. As for the kasra, al-Farra' claimed that it is made similar to the Arabic expression "jair, la af'alu" (by Allah, I will not do it), so on this view "Yasini" is an oath, and Ibn Abbas said so. It was also said: it is made similar to amsi, Hadhaam, ha'ulaa' and Raqash. As for the damma, it is made similar to mundhu, haythu and qatt, and to the vocative singular when you say "ya rajulu," for the one who pauses upon it. Ibn al-Sumaiqa and Harun said: It has been explained as "ya rajul," so the damma is the more fitting for it. Ibn al-Anbari said: "Yasin" is a good pause for those who say it is the opening of the surah; and for those who say the meaning of "Yasin" is "ya rajul," he does not pause upon it. It is related from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and others that its meaning is "ya insan" (O human being). O soul, do not exhaust yourself in sincere advice, striving,
and upon affection, except the family of Yasin.

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: Its meaning is "O master of mankind." It was also said: It is one of the names of Allah. Malik said, and Ashhab related from him: I asked him, "Is it fitting for anyone to name himself Yasin?" Ibn al-‘Arabi said: This is a wonderful statement, for a servant may name himself with a name of the Lord if there is in it a meaning from Him, such as "knowing," "powerful," "willing," and "speaking." Malik only forbade naming with "Yasin" because it is one of the names of Allah whose meaning is not known, so perhaps its meaning is something exclusive to the Lord, and it is not permissible for the servant to presume upon it. Some scholars said: Allah opened this surah with the letters ya and sin, and in them is the gathering of goodness. The opening indicates that it is a heart, and the heart is the ruler of the body; likewise "Ya-Sin" is the ruler over the rest of the surahs, encompassing the whole Qur'an. Sibawayh mentioned the fatha and gave it two aspects: one is that it is an object and is not declined, because it is for him a foreign noun like Habil, the implied sense being "Remember Yasina." Sibawayh made it the name of the surah. The other aspect is that it is indeclinable upon fatha, like kayfa and ayna. As for the kasra, al-Farra' claimed that it is made similar to the Arabic expression "jair, la af'alu" (by Allah, I will not do it), so on this view "Yasini" is an oath, and Ibn Abbas said so. It was also said: it is made similar to amsi, Hadhaam, ha'ulaa' and Raqash. As for the damma, it is made similar to mundhu, haythu and qatt, and to the vocative singular when you say "ya rajulu," for the one who pauses upon it. Ibn al-Sumaiqa and Harun said: It has been explained as "ya rajul," so the damma is the more fitting for it. Ibn al-Anbari said: "Yasin" is a good pause for those who say it is the opening of the surah; and for those who say the meaning of "Yasin" is "ya rajul," he does not pause upon it. It is related from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and others that its meaning is "ya insan" (O human being). They said of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Peace upon the family of Yasin﴾ [al-Saffat: 130], that it means "upon the family of Muhammad." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: It is one of the names of Muhammad (ﷺ), and its proof is "Indeed you are among the messengers." Al-Sayyid al-Himyari said:

O soul, do not exhaust yourself in sincere advice, striving,
and upon affection, except the family of Yasin.

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: Its meaning is "O master of mankind." It was also said: It is one of the names of Allah. Malik said, and Ashhab related from him: I asked him, "Is it fitting for anyone to name himself Yasin?" He said: "I do not think it is fitting, because of the words of Allah: 'Ya-Sin, wal-Qur'ani l-Hakim,' as if he says, 'This is My name, Yasin.'" Ibn al-‘Arabi said: This is a wonderful statement, for a servant may name himself with a name of the Lord if there is in it a meaning from Him, such as "knowing," "powerful," "willing," and "speaking." Malik only forbade naming with "Yasin" because it is one of the names of Allah whose meaning is not known, so perhaps its meaning is something exclusive to the Lord, and it is not permissible for the servant to presume upon it. If it is said: Allah, Exalted is He, has said: ﴿Peace upon the family of Yasin﴾ [al-Saffat: 130]. We say: That is written with its spelling (hijaʼ), so naming with it is permitted, and this which is not spelled out is what Malik spoke about, because of the difficulty in it, and Allah knows best. The opening indicates that it is a heart, and the heart is the ruler of the body; likewise "Ya-Sin" is the ruler over the rest of the surahs, encompassing the whole Qur'an. Al-Kalbi: It is in Syriac, and the Arabs spoke it so it became part of their language. This meaning has already passed in [Ta-Ha] and in the introduction of the book, in full. Al-Qadi Iyad has laid out the views of the exegetes on the meaning of "Yasin." Abu Muhammad Makki related that it was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I have ten names with my Lord," and he mentioned that among them are Ta-Ha and Yasin, which are two of his names.

Qurtubi said: Al-Mawardi reported from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Allah the Exalted named me in the Qur'an with seven names: Muhammad, Ahmad, Ta-Ha, Ya-Sin, al-Muzzammil, al-Muddaththir, and Abdullah.'" Al-Zajjaj said: it has been said its meaning is "O Muhammad," and it has been said "O man," and it has been said "O human being." And from Ibn al-Hanafiyyah: "Ya-Sin" means "O Muhammad." And from Ka'b: "Ya-Sin" is an oath which Allah swore by before He created the heavens and the earth by two thousand years, [[An addition required by the context, and supported by what is related in al-Durr al-Manthur of al-Suyuti from Ka'b.]] "O Muhammad, indeed you are among the messengers" (ﷺ), then He said: "By the Wise Qur'an."

And if it is in the sense of a call, then another oath has come after it, to confirm his messengership and to bear witness to his guidance. Allah the Exalted swore by His name and His Book: "Indeed you are among the messengers," through His revelation to His servants, "on a straight path," from His faith, meaning a path with no crookedness in it and no deviation from the truth.

Al-Naqqash said: Allah the Exalted did not swear for any of His prophets concerning messengership in His Book except for him, and in it is of his exaltation and glorification according to the interpretation of whoever says it means "O master," as is in it; and he (peace be upon him) said: "I am the master of the children of Adam." Al-Qushayri related that Ibn Abbas said: The disbelievers of Quraysh said, "You are not a messenger, and Allah has not sent you to us," so Allah swore by the firm (muhkam) Qur'an that Muhammad is among the messengers. Likewise it is made firm in its composition and its meanings, so no flaw reaches it. "Al-Hakim" in reference to Allah may mean "al-muhkim" with a kasra on the kaf, like "al-alim" meaning "al-mu'lim" (the one who causes pain). His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful﴾. Ibn Amir, Hafs, al-A'mash, Yahya, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "tanzila" with a fatha on the lam, as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: Allah sent down that as a sending down. It is said: Allah sent the rain and sent it down, with the same meaning. Muhammad (ﷺ) is the mercy of Allah, which He sent down from the heaven. And whoever reads it with a fatha says: "Indeed you are among the messengers" by a sending from the Mighty, the Merciful. "Al-Aziz" means the one who takes vengeance upon whoever opposes Him, and "al-Rahim" means the one who is merciful toward the people of His obedience.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah Yasin. It is Meccan by unanimous consensus. It has eighty-three verses, except that a group said that His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And We record what they have sent before and their traces﴾ [Yasin: 12] was revealed concerning the Banu Salima of the Ansar when they wanted to leave their dwellings and move near the Mosque of the Messenger (ﷺ), as will come. In the Sunan of Abu Dawud, on the authority of Ma'qil ibn Yasar, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Recite Yasin over your dead." Al-Ajurri mentioned, from the hadith of Umm al-Darda' [[So it is in all the copies of the original; what is in al-Durr al-Manthur is Abi al-Darda'.]], on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "There is no dead person over whom Surah Yasin is recited except that Allah lightens it for him." In the Musnad of al-Darimi, on the authority of Abu Hurairah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Surah Yasin in a night seeking the Face of Allah, he will be forgiven in that night." Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz also related it. Al-Tirmidhi related, on the authority of Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Yasin. Whoever recites Yasin, Allah records for him by its recitation the reward of reading the Qur'an ten times." He said: This is a gharib hadith, and in its chain is Harun Abu Muhammad, an unknown shaykh. And concerning this chapter there is also a report from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, but the hadith of Abu Bakr is not sound in terms of its chain, and its chain is weak. And on the authority of Aisha that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed in the Qur'an there is a surah that intercedes for its reciters and whose listeners are forgiven. Behold, it is Surah Yasin, and it is called in the Torah al-Mu'imma." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is al-Mu'imma?" He said: "It encompasses its companion with the good of this world and repels from him the terrors of the Hereafter, and it is called al-Dafi'a and al-Qadiya." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, how is that?" He said: "It repels from its companion every evil and fulfils for him every need. Whoever recites it, it counts for him as twenty pilgrimages; whoever hears it, it is for him like a thousand dinars given in charity in the way of Allah; and whoever writes it and drinks it, it enters his belly as a thousand cures, a thousand lights, a thousand certainties, a thousand mercies, a thousand compassions, a thousand guidances, and removes from him every disease and rancor." Al-Tha'labi mentioned it from the hadith of Aisha, and al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim in Nawadir al-Usul mentioned it from the hadith of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, as a musnad report. In the Musnad of al-Darimi, on the authority of Shahr ibn Hawshab, who said: Ibn Abbas said: "Whoever recites Yasin in the morning is given the ease of his day until evening, and whoever recites it at the beginning of his night is given the ease of his night until morning." Al-Nahhas mentioned, on the authority of Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, who said: "For everything there is a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Yasin. Whoever recites it by day, his concern is relieved, and whoever recites it by night, his sin is forgiven." Shahr ibn Hawshab said: The people of Paradise recite only Ta-Ha and Yasin. Al-Mawardi raised these three reports to the Prophet, saying: Al-Dahhak related on the authority of Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Yasin. Whoever recites it in a night is given the ease of that night, and whoever recites it in a day is given the ease of that day. Indeed the people of Paradise will have the Qur'an lifted from them, so they will recite nothing but Ta-Ha and Yasin." Yahya ibn Abi Kathir said: "It has reached me that whoever recites Surah Yasin at night will remain in joy until morning, and whoever recites it in the morning will remain in joy until evening, and someone who tested it has related to me." Al-Tha'labi and Ibn Atiyya mentioned it. Ibn Atiyya said: Experience confirms this. Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim in Nawadir al-Usul mentioned, on the authority of Abd al-A'la, who said: Muhammad ibn al-Salt related to us from Umar ibn Thabit, from Muhammad ibn Marwan, from Abu Ja'far, who said: "Whoever finds hardness in his heart, let him write Yasin in a cup with saffron and then drink it." My father, may Allah have mercy on him, related to me, saying: Asram ibn Hawshab related to us, from Baqiyya ibn al-Walid, from al-Mu'tamir ibn Ashraf, from Muhammad ibn Ali, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Qur'an is better than everything apart from Allah, and the excellence of the Qur'an over other speech is like the excellence of Allah over His creation. Whoever honours the Qur'an has honoured Allah, and whoever does not honour the Qur'an has not honoured Allah. The sanctity of the Qur'an before Allah is like the sanctity of a father over his son. The Qur'an is an intercessor whose intercession is accepted, and an advocate whose testimony is believed. Whoever the Qur'an intercedes for, it is granted; whoever it argues against, it prevails over. Whoever makes it his leader, it leads him to Paradise; whoever makes it his follower, it drives him to the Fire." The bearers of the Qur'an are those surrounded by the sanctity of Allah, clothed in the light of Allah, taught the speech of Allah. Whoever befriends them has befriended Allah, and whoever opposes them has opposed Allah. Allah, Exalted is He, says: "O bearers of the Qur'an, respond to your Lord by honouring His Book, and He will increase you in love and make you beloved to His servants. The trials of this world are repelled from the listener of the Qur'an, and the trials of the Hereafter are repelled from its reciter. Whoever hears a verse from the Book of Allah, it is better for him than what is beneath the Throne down to the earth. Indeed in the Book of Allah there is a surah called al-Aziza, and its companion will be called al-Sharif on the Day of Resurrection; it will intercede for its companion for more than the tribes of Rabi'a and Mudar, and it is Surah Yasin." Al-Tha'labi mentioned, on the authority of Abu Hurairah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Surah Yasin on Friday night will wake up forgiven." And on the authority of Anas, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever enters the graveyards and recites Surah Yasin, Allah lightens the punishment for them that day, and he will have as many good deeds as the number of its letters."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 36, verses 6–8:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So that you may warn a people whose forefathers were not warned, so they are heedless﴾. Regarding "qawman" (a people), most exegetes, including Qatadah, hold that it has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis), because it is a negation. The meaning is: "so that you may warn a people to whom no warner came before you, to their forefathers." It has also been said that it is in the sense of "alladhi" (which), so the meaning is: "so that you may warn them with the same warning that their forefathers received." This was said by Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah and Qatadah as well. It has also been said that "qawman" and the verb form a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: "so that you may warn a people with the warning of their forefathers." It is also possible that the Arabs had received reports of the prophets through continuous transmission (tawatur), so the meaning is that they were not warned by a messenger from among themselves. It is also possible that the report had reached them, but they were negligent, turned away and forgot. It is also possible that this is an address to a people to whom the news of no prophet had reached, and Allah has said: ﴿We did not give them any scriptures to study, nor did We send them any warner before you﴾ [Saba: 44], and He said: ﴿So that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you, so that they may be guided﴾ [As-Sajdah: 3], meaning: no prophet had come to them. According to the view of those who say that the news of the prophets had reached them, the meaning of "fahum ghafilun" is that they are turning away and are now heedless of that. It is said of one who turns away from something that he is heedless of it. It has also been said that "fahum ghafilun" means they are heedless of the punishment of Allah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed the word has come into effect against most of them﴾, meaning the punishment has become obligatory for most of them. "So they do not believe" in your warning. This applies to those whom Allah's knowledge foreknew would die in their disbelief. Then He explained the cause of their refusal to believe, saying: ﴿Indeed, We have put shackles around their necks﴾. It was said: it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl ibn Hisham and his two Makhzumi companions. Abu Jahl swore that if he saw Muhammad (ﷺ) praying, he would crush his head with a rock. When he saw him, he went and raised a rock to throw it, but when he gestured toward him, his hand returned to his neck and the rock stuck to his hand. This was related by Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah and others. Thus, according to this, it is a metaphor, meaning that he was like one whose hand is chained to his neck. When he returned to his companions and told them what he had seen, the second man, who was al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, said: "I will crush his head." He came to him while he (ﷺ) was praying in the same state, to throw the rock at him, but Allah blinded his sight, so he began to hear his voice without seeing him. He returned to his companions, but did not see them until they called out to him. He said: "By Allah, I did not see him, but I heard his voice." The third man said: "By Allah, I will smash his head myself." He took the rock and set off, but he came back backwards, retreating on his heels, until he fell on his back, unconscious. He was asked: "What is wrong with you?" He said: "My condition is grave. I saw the man, and when I drew near to him, there was a stallion swishing its tail. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 36, verses 9–11:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We have placed a barrier before them and a barrier behind them﴾. Muqatil said: When Abu Jahl returned to his companions without having reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and the stone had fallen from his hand, another man from the Banu Makhzum took the stone and said: "I will kill him with this stone." When he drew near to the Prophet (ﷺ), Allah blinded his sight, so he did not see the Prophet (ﷺ). He returned to his companions but could not see them until they called out to him. This is the meaning of the verse.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said in his narration: Utbah and Shaybah, the sons of Rabi'ah, Abu Jahl, and Umayyah ibn Khalaf sat in wait for the Prophet (ﷺ) in order to inflict harm upon him. He (ﷺ) came out to them while reciting "Ya-Sin," and there was dust in his hand, which he threw at them, and he recited: ﴿And We have placed a barrier before them and a barrier behind them﴾. They lowered their heads until he (ﷺ) passed by them. This has already been discussed in the surah of "Subhan" [[See vol. 10, p. 269, first or second edition.]], and it was discussed in "al-Kahf" [[See vol. 11, p. 59, first or second edition.]] regarding "sudda," with the sin pronounced with a damma or with a fatha, both being dialectal forms.

﴿So We have covered them﴾, i.e., We covered their sight. This has already been discussed at the beginning of [al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 191, second or third edition.]]]. Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, and Yahya ibn Ya'mur read "fa-a'shaynahum" with an unpointed ʿayn, from al-ʿashaʾ (night blindness) in the eye, which is the weakness of its sight such that it cannot see at night. The poet said:

Whenever you come to him, you squint toward the light of his fire,
You will find the best fire there, and the best kindler.
[This is al-Hutay'ah; the complete verse is: "You will find the best fire there, and the best kindler."]

And Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 36], and so on. The meanings are close, and the meaning is "We blinded them," as the poet said:

And among the calamities, may you have no father, is that I
And the earth has been struck upon me with barriers,
I do not find my way in it to the place of a hill-path,
Between al-Adhb and the land of Murad.

﴿So they do not see﴾, i.e., the guidance, said by Qatadah. It was also said: it means Muhammad, when they conspired to kill him, said by al-Suddi. Al-Dahhak said: ﴿And We have placed a barrier before them﴾ means this world, ﴿and a barrier behind them﴾ means the Hereafter; that is, they were blind to the Resurrection and blind to accepting the laws in this world. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We appointed for them companions who made attractive to them what was before them and what was behind them﴾, i.e., they made the world attractive to them and called them to deny the Hereafter. It was also said, on this view: ﴿before them a barrier﴾ means deception by the world, and ﴿behind them a barrier﴾ means denial of the Hereafter. It was also said: ﴿before them﴾ means the Hereafter, and ﴿behind them﴾ means this world.

﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾ has been discussed in [al-Baqarah [[See vol. 8, p. 184, second or third edition.]]]. This verse is a refutation of the Qadariyyah (those who deny divine predestination) and others.

When he drew near to the Prophet (ﷺ), Allah blinded his sight, so he did not see the Prophet (ﷺ). He returned to his companions but could not see them until they called out to him. This is the meaning of the verse.

He (ﷺ) came out to them while reciting "Ya-Sin," and there was dust in his hand, which he threw at them, and he recited: ﴿And We have placed a barrier before them and a barrier behind them﴾. They lowered their heads until he (ﷺ) passed by them. This has already been discussed in the surah of "Subhan" [[See vol. 10, p. 269, first or second edition.]], and it was discussed in "al-Kahf" [[See vol. 11, p. 59, first or second edition.]] regarding "sudda," with the sin pronounced with a damma or with a fatha, both being dialectal forms.

﴿So We have covered them﴾, i.e., We covered their sight. This has already been discussed at the beginning of [al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 191, second or third edition.]]]. The poet said:

Whenever you come to him, you squint toward the light of his fire,
You will find the best fire there, and the best kindler.
[This is al-Hutay'ah; the complete verse is: "You will find the best fire there, and the best kindler."]

And Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 36], and so on. The meanings are close, and the meaning is "We blinded them," as the poet said:

And among the calamities, may you have no father, is that I
And the earth has been struck upon me with barriers,
I do not find my way in it to the place of a hill-path,
Between al-Adhb and the land of Murad.

The first matter: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it is We who give life to the dead﴾. He informed us of His giving life to the dead in response to the disbelievers. Al-Dahhak and al-Hasan said: that is, He gives them life through faith after ignorance. The first interpretation is more apparent, that is, He gives them life through resurrection for recompense. Then He threatened them by mentioning that He records their traces (al-athar), and the recording and counting (ihsa') of everything and of all that a person does.

Qatadah said: its meaning is "of deeds." Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said the same. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿A soul will know what it has sent forward and what it has left behind﴾ (al-Infitar: 5), and His saying: ﴿On that Day man will be informed of what he sent forward and left behind﴾ (al-Qiyamah: 13), and He said: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah, and let every soul look to what it has put forward for tomorrow﴾ (al-Hashr: 18). So a person's traces are those that remain and are remembered after him, whether good or evil, for which he is recompensed. Of good traces: a knowledge he taught, a book he authored, an endowment (habis) he set aside, or a building he erected, such as a mosque, a ribat (a fortified lodge for travellers and devotees), a bridge, or the like. Of bad traces: an impost that some oppressors levied on the Muslims, a coin they minted which caused them loss, or something they introduced which turns people away from the remembrance of Allah, such as singing and amusements. Likewise every good practice or evil practice that is followed.

It was also said: they are the traces of those who walk to the mosques. Umar, Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr interpreted the verse according to this meaning. It is also reported from Ibn Abbas that the meaning of "their traces" is their steps to the mosques. Al-Nahhas said: this is the best of what has been said about it, because it was said that the verse was revealed concerning this, since the Ansar's dwellings were far from the mosque.

In a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "For him one good deed is written for each step, and one evil is removed from him, going and returning, when he goes out to the mosque."

I say: In al-Tirmidhi, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, he said: The Banu Salamah [[Salamah, with a kasra on the lam, is a clan of the Ansar.]] were in a district of Madinah, and they wished to move closer to the mosque, so this verse was revealed: "Indeed, it is We who give life to the dead, and We record what they have sent forward and their traces." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed your traces are recorded," so they did not move. He said: This is a hasan gharib hadith from the narration of al-Thawri. [[The addition is from the Sahih of al-Tirmidhi.]]

In Sahih Muslim, from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, he said: The Banu Salamah wished to relocate closer to the mosque. He said: The open land was empty. He said: This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "O Banu Salamah, stay in your dwellings; your traces are recorded. Stay in your dwellings; your traces are recorded." They said: "It would not have pleased us that we had moved."

Thabit al-Bunani said: I walked with Anas ibn Malik to the prayer and hastened, and he held me back. When the prayer was finished he said: I walked with the Prophet (ﷺ) and hastened, and he held me back. When the prayer was finished he said: "Do you not know that traces are recorded?" So this is an argument from the verse.

Qatadah, Mujahid also, and al-Hasan said: the traces in this verse are the steps. Al-Tha'labi reported from Anas that he said: the traces are the steps to Friday prayer.

The singular of athar is athar, and it is also said athr.

The third matter: These hadiths explaining the meaning of the verse are evidence that distance from the mosque is more excellent. So if one lives next to a mosque, may he pass it to a more distant one? This has been disputed. It is reported from Anas that he used to pass the nearer mosque for the older one. It is reported from others: the farther a mosque is from one's home, the greater its reward. Al-Hasan and others disliked this and said: one should not leave the mosque nearest to him and go to another. This is the position of Malik. Regarding passing one's own mosque for the grand mosque (the congregational mosque), there are two opinions.

Ibn Majah transmitted from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man's prayer in his house counts as one prayer; his prayer in the mosque of the tribes counts as twenty-five prayers; and his prayer in the mosque where the Friday congregation is gathered [[yujamma' (with tashdid), from the gathering, meaning the Friday prayer is performed in it.]] counts as five hundred prayers."

"Diyarakum" is in the accusative by way of incitement (al-igra'), meaning: "Remain." And "naktub" is in the jussive as an answer to that command. "Kulla" is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb indicated by "ahsaynahu," as if he said: "And We counted everything, We counted it." It is permissible to read it in the nominative as a beginning (mubtada'), but the accusative is preferable, so that what the verb governs is coordinated with what the verb governs. This is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh.

Al-Imam: the book to be followed, which is a proof. Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: it means the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). A group said: it means the pages of deeds.

This is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ. He was commanded to set forth for his people the example of the people of the town ([The addition is from the marginal note of Hashiyat Jamal on Ibn 'Aqil's commentary.]). According to the opinion of all the exegetes, as al-Mawardi reported, this town is Antioch. It was named after the people of Antabis, which was the name of the one who built it, and then it was altered when it was Arabized. Al-Suhayli mentioned this. It is also said as Antakiya, with a ta' in place of the ta'. There was a Pharaoh in it called Antikhus son of Antikhus, who worshipped idols. Al-Mahdawi mentioned this, and Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas related it from Ka'b and Wahb. Allah sent to it three messengers: Sadiq, Sadduq, and Shalum, who was the third. This is the statement of al-Tabari. Others said: Shim'un and Yuhanna. Al-Naqqash related: Sam'an and Yahya, and he did not mention Sadiq or Sadduq.

It is permissible for "mathalan" (an example) and "ashab al-qarya" (the people of the town) to be two objects of "idrib" (set forth), or for "ashab al-qarya" to be an apposition to "mathalan," meaning: set forth for them the example of the people of the town, with the genitive omitted (hadhf al-mudaf).

The Prophet ﷺ was commanded to warn these polytheists that there should befall them what befell the disbelievers of the people of the town, to whom three messengers were sent.

It was said: they were messengers from Allah from the outset. It was also said: Jesus sent them to Antioch to call to Allah. The Lord attributed that to Himself, because Jesus had sent them by the command of the Lord, and that was when Jesus was raised to heaven. It was said: they struck them and imprisoned them.

"Fa-'azzaznā bi-thālith" (then We strengthened with a third): that is, We strengthened and reinforced the message with a third.

Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read "fa-'azazna" with the lightened form, and the rest read it with the intensified form. Al-Jawhari said: The saying of the Exalted, "fa-'azzaznā bi-thālith," is read with and without the intensification (tashdid), meaning: We strengthened and reinforced. Al-Asma'i said: Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' recited to me in it, for al-Mutalammis:

"Ujudd idhā rahalat ta'azzaza laḥmuhā... wa-idhā tushuddu bi-nis'ihā lā tanbis"

That is: when she is ridden, her flesh becomes firm, and when she is girded with her saddle-girth, she does not bellow. That means she does not roar; on this basis the two readings have the same meaning. It was also said: the lightened form means "we overcame and subdued," and from it is the saying, "wa-'azzani fi al-khiṭāb" (and he overpowered me in argument). The intensified form means "we strengthened and multiplied."

In the story: Jesus sent two messengers to them. They met an old man tending his small flock, who was Habib the carpenter, the companion of "Ya Sin." They called him to Allah and said: We are the messengers of Jesus; we call you to the worship of Allah. He demanded of them a miracle, and they said: We heal the sick. He had a son who was insane. It was also said he was sick and bedridden, so they wiped over him, and he rose healthy by the permission of Allah. The man then believed in Allah.

It was also said: he is the one who came from the farthest part of the city running (Ya Sin 36:20). Their matter spread, and they healed many of the sick. So the king, who worshipped idols, sent for them to question them. They said: We are the messengers of Jesus. He said: What is your sign? They said: We heal the blind and the leper, and we heal the sick by the permission of Allah, and we call you to the worship of Allah alone. The king was resolved to strike them.

Wahb said: the king imprisoned them and flogged them one hundred lashes. The news reached Jesus, so he sent a third. It was said: Shim'un al-Safa', the head of the disciples, to support them. He associated with the king's courtiers until he gained their confidence; they took to him and related his talk to the king, and the king became fond of him and showed agreement with his religion. The king approved of his conduct. Then one day he said to the king: It has reached me that you have imprisoned two men who called you to Allah. If you were to ask about them, you would learn what lies behind them. The king said: Anger prevented me from questioning them. He said: If you were to bring them forth... So he ordered that, and Shim'un said to them: What is your proof for what you claim? They said: We heal the blind and the leper. A boy whose eyes had been wiped away was brought, the place of his eyes being like a forehead. They called upon their Lord, and the place of sight split open. They took two balls of clay and placed them in his cheeks, and they became two eyeballs with which he saw. The king was astonished and said: Here is a boy who died seven days ago and whom I have not buried, until his father comes. Can your Lord bring him back to life? They called upon Allah openly, and Shim'un called upon Him in secret, and the dead boy rose alive. He said to the people: I died seven days ago, and I was found to be a polytheist, so I was made to enter seven valleys of fire. I warn you of what you are in, so believe in Allah. Then the doors of heaven were opened, and I saw a handsome young man interceding for these three, Shim'un and his two companions, until Allah revived me. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah alone, with no partner, and that Jesus is the spirit of Allah and His word, and that these are the messengers of Allah. They said to him: And is this Shim'un with them too? He said: Yes, and he is the best of them. Shim'un then informed them that he was the messenger of the Messiah to them. His words had an effect on the king, so he called him to Allah, and the king believed, together with a great many people, while others disbelieved.

Al-Qushayri related that the king believed but his people did not believe, and Gabriel cried out one cry, and every disbeliever who remained among them died.

It is also related that when Jesus commanded them to go to that town, they said: O Prophet of Allah, we do not know how to speak in their tongues and dialects. So he prayed to Allah for them, and they slept where they were. Then they awoke from their sleep, the angels having carried them and placed them in the land of Antioch. Each of them spoke to his companion in the language of the people, and that is the saying of Allah, "And We supported him with the Holy Spirit" (2:87). Then they all said: "Indeed, we are sent to you" (36:14). They said: "You are not but men like us; you eat food and walk in the markets" (36:15), "and the Most Merciful has revealed nothing; you are only lying" (36:15), in your claim of being messengers. "Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you" (36:16). The messengers said: "Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you," even if you deny us. "And upon us is only the clear notification" (36:17) that Allah is One. "They said," to them, "Indeed, we consider you a bad omen" (36:18), that is, we consider you inauspicious.

Muqatil said: rain was withheld from them for three years, so they said: This is because of your ill omen. It is also said that they remained warning them for ten years. "If you do not desist" (36:18) from our warning, "we will surely stone you" (36:18). Al-Farra' said: we will surely kill you. He said: most of what is in the Qur'an concerning rajm (stoning) means killing. Qatadah said: it is literal, stoning with stones. It was also said: we will surely revile you. All of this has already been mentioned ([See vol. 9, p. 91, first or second edition.]). "And a painful punishment will surely touch you from us" (36:18). It was said: it is killing. It was said: it is painful torment. It was also said: it is painful torment before killing, such as flaying, cutting off, and crucifixion.

Then the messengers said: "Your omen is with you" (36:19), that is, your ill omen is with you, meaning your share of good and evil is with you and clings to your necks, and it is not from our ill omen. This was the statement of al-Dahhak. Qatadah said: your deeds are with you. Ibn 'Abbas said: its meaning is that provisions and decrees follow you. Al-Farra' said: "Your omen is with you" means your provision and your deeds, and the meaning is one.

Al-Hasan read "aṭṭayrukum" (your ill omen), meaning your taṭayyur (the act of considering omens) ([Abu Hayyan said regarding this reading: "aṭṭayrukum" is a verbal noun of "aṭṭayara," in which the ta' was assimilated into the ṭa', so the hamzat al-wasl (connecting hamza) was introduced in the past tense and the verbal noun.]). They called him to Allah and said: We are the messengers of Jesus; we call you to the worship of Allah. He demanded of them a miracle, and they said: We heal the sick. He had a son who was insane. It was also said he was sick and bedridden, so they wiped over him, and he rose healthy by the permission of Allah. The man then believed in Allah.

It was also said: he is the one who came from the farthest part of the city running (Ya Sin 36:20). Their matter spread, and they healed many of the sick. So the king, who worshipped idols, sent for them to question them. They said: We are the messengers of Jesus. He said: What is your sign? They said: We heal the blind and the leper, and we heal the sick by the permission of Allah, and we call you to the worship of Allah alone. The king was resolved to strike them.

Wahb said: the king imprisoned them and flogged them one hundred lashes. The news reached Jesus, so he sent a third. It was said: Shim'un al-Safa', the head of the disciples, to support them. He associated with the king's courtiers until he gained their confidence; they took to him and related his talk to the king, and the king became fond of him and showed agreement with his religion. The king approved of his conduct. Then one day he said to the king: It has reached me that you have imprisoned two men who called you to Allah. If you were to ask about them, you would learn what lies behind them. The king said: Anger prevented me from questioning them. He said: If you were to bring them forth... So he ordered that, and Shim'un said to them: What is your proof for what you claim? They said: We heal the blind and the leper. A boy whose eyes had been wiped away was brought, the place of his eyes being like a forehead. They called upon their Lord, and the place of sight split open. They took two balls of clay and placed them in his cheeks, and they became two eyeballs with which he saw. The king was astonished and said: Here is a boy who died seven days ago and whom I have not buried, until his father comes. Can your Lord bring him back to life? They called upon Allah openly, and Shim'un called upon Him in secret, and the dead boy rose alive. He said to the people: I died seven days ago, and I was found to be a polytheist, so I was made to enter seven valleys of fire. I warn you of what you are in, so believe in Allah. Then the doors of heaven were opened, and I saw a handsome young man interceding for these three, Shim'un and his two companions, until Allah revived me. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah alone, with no partner, and that Jesus is the spirit of Allah and His word, and that these are the messengers of Allah. They said to him: And is this Shim'un with them too? He said: Yes, and he is the best of them. Shim'un then informed them that he was the messenger of the Messiah to them. His words had an effect on the king, so he called him to Allah, and the king believed, together with a great many people, while others disbelieved.

Al-Qushayri related that the king believed but his people did not believe, and Gabriel cried out one cry, and every disbeliever who remained among them died.

It is also related that when Jesus commanded them to go to that town, they said: O Prophet of Allah, we do not know how to speak in their tongues and dialects. Then they all said: "Indeed, we are sent to you" (36:14). They said: "You are not but men like us; you eat food and walk in the markets" (36:15), "and the Most Merciful has revealed nothing; you are only lying" (36:15), in your claim of being messengers.
