He was commanded to set forth for his people the example of the people of the town ([The addition is from the marginal note of Hashiyat Jamal on Ibn 'Aqil's commentary.]). According to the opinion of all the exegetes, as al-Mawardi reported, this town is Antioch. It was named after the people of Antabis, which was the name of the one who built it, and then it was altered when it was Arabized. Al-Suhayli mentioned this. It is also said as Antakiya, with a ta' in place of the ta'. There was a Pharaoh in it called Antikhus son of Antikhus, who worshipped idols. Al-Mahdawi mentioned this, and Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas related it from Ka'b and Wahb. Allah sent to it three messengers: Sadiq, Sadduq, and Shalum, who was the third. This is the statement of al-Tabari. Others said: Shim'un and Yuhanna. Al-Naqqash related: Sam'an and Yahya, and he did not mention Sadiq or Sadduq.

It is permissible for "mathalan" (an example) and "ashab al-qarya" (the people of the town) to be two objects of "idrib" (set forth), or for "ashab al-qarya" to be an apposition to "mathalan," meaning: set forth for them the example of the people of the town, with the genitive omitted (hadhf al-mudaf).

The Prophet ﷺ was commanded to warn these polytheists that there should befall them what befell the disbelievers of the people of the town, to whom three messengers were sent.

It was said: they were messengers from Allah from the outset. It was also said: Jesus sent them to Antioch to call to Allah. The Lord attributed that to Himself, because Jesus had sent them by the command of the Lord, and that was when Jesus was raised to heaven. It was said: they struck them and imprisoned them.

"Fa-'azzaznā bi-thālith" (then We strengthened with a third): that is, We strengthened and reinforced the message with a third.

Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read "fa-'azazna" with the lightened form, and the rest read it with the intensified form. Al-Jawhari said: The saying of the Exalted, "fa-'azzaznā bi-thālith," is read with and without the intensification (tashdid), meaning: We strengthened and reinforced. Al-Asma'i said: Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' recited to me in it, for al-Mutalammis:

"Ujudd idhā rahalat ta'azzaza laḥmuhā... wa-idhā tushuddu bi-nis'ihā lā tanbis"

That is: when she is ridden, her flesh becomes firm, and when she is girded with her saddle-girth, she does not bellow. That means she does not roar; on this basis the two readings have the same meaning. It was also said: the lightened form means "we overcame and subdued," and from it is the saying, "wa-'azzani fi al-khiṭāb" (and he overpowered me in argument). The intensified form means "we strengthened and multiplied."

In the story: Jesus sent two messengers to them. They met an old man tending his small flock, who was Habib the carpenter, the companion of "Ya Sin." They called him to Allah and said: We are the messengers of Jesus; we call you to the worship of Allah. He demanded of them a miracle, and they said: We heal the sick. He had a son who was insane. It was also said he was sick and bedridden, so they wiped over him, and he rose healthy by the permission of Allah. The man then believed in Allah.

It was also said: he is the one who came from the farthest part of the city running (Ya Sin 36:20). Their matter spread, and they healed many of the sick. So the king, who worshipped idols, sent for them to question them. They said: We are the messengers of Jesus. He said: What is your sign? They said: We heal the blind and the leper, and we heal the sick by the permission of Allah, and we call you to the worship of Allah alone. The king was resolved to strike them.

Wahb said: the king imprisoned them and flogged them one hundred lashes. The news reached Jesus, so he sent a third. It was said: Shim'un al-Safa', the head of the disciples, to support them. He associated with the king's courtiers until he gained their confidence; they took to him and related his talk to the king, and the king became fond of him and showed agreement with his religion. The king approved of his conduct. Then one day he said to the king: It has reached me that you have imprisoned two men who called you to Allah. If you were to ask about them, you would learn what lies behind them. The king said: Anger prevented me from questioning them. He said: If you were to bring them forth... So he ordered that, and Shim'un said to them: What is your proof for what you claim? They said: We heal the blind and the leper. A boy whose eyes had been wiped away was brought, the place of his eyes being like a forehead. They called upon their Lord, and the place of sight split open. They took two balls of clay and placed them in his cheeks, and they became two eyeballs with which he saw. The king was astonished and said: Here is a boy who died seven days ago and whom I have not buried, until his father comes. Can your Lord bring him back to life? They called upon Allah openly, and Shim'un called upon Him in secret, and the dead boy rose alive. He said to the people: I died seven days ago, and I was found to be a polytheist, so I was made to enter seven valleys of fire. I warn you of what you are in, so believe in Allah. Then the doors of heaven were opened, and I saw a handsome young man interceding for these three, Shim'un and his two companions, until Allah revived me. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah alone, with no partner, and that Jesus is the spirit of Allah and His word, and that these are the messengers of Allah. They said to him: And is this Shim'un with them too? He said: Yes, and he is the best of them. Shim'un then informed them that he was the messenger of the Messiah to them. His words had an effect on the king, so he called him to Allah, and the king believed, together with a great many people, while others disbelieved.

Al-Qushayri related that the king believed but his people did not believe, and Gabriel cried out one cry, and every disbeliever who remained among them died.

It is also related that when Jesus commanded them to go to that town, they said: O Prophet of Allah, we do not know how to speak in their tongues and dialects. So he prayed to Allah for them, and they slept where they were. Then they awoke from their sleep, the angels having carried them and placed them in the land of Antioch. Each of them spoke to his companion in the language of the people, and that is the saying of Allah, "And We supported him with the Holy Spirit" (2:87). Then they all said: "Indeed, we are sent to you" (36:14). They said: "You are not but men like us; you eat food and walk in the markets" (36:15), "and the Most Merciful has revealed nothing; you are only lying" (36:15), in your claim of being messengers. "Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you" (36:16). The messengers said: "Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you," even if you deny us. "And upon us is only the clear notification" (36:17) that Allah is One. "They said," to them, "Indeed, we consider you a bad omen" (36:18), that is, we consider you inauspicious.

Muqatil said: rain was withheld from them for three years, so they said: This is because of your ill omen. It is also said that they remained warning them for ten years. "If you do not desist" (36:18) from our warning, "we will surely stone you" (36:18). Al-Farra' said: we will surely kill you. He said: most of what is in the Qur'an concerning rajm (stoning) means killing. Qatadah said: it is literal, stoning with stones. It was also said: we will surely revile you. All of this has already been mentioned ([See vol. 9, p. 91, first or second edition.]). "And a painful punishment will surely touch you from us" (36:18). It was said: it is killing. It was said: it is painful torment. It was also said: it is painful torment before killing, such as flaying, cutting off, and crucifixion.

Then the messengers said: "Your omen is with you" (36:19), that is, your ill omen is with you, meaning your share of good and evil is with you and clings to your necks, and it is not from our ill omen. This was the statement of al-Dahhak. Qatadah said: your deeds are with you. Ibn 'Abbas said: its meaning is that provisions and decrees follow you. Al-Farra' said: "Your omen is with you" means your provision and your deeds, and the meaning is one.

Al-Hasan read "aṭṭayrukum" (your ill omen), meaning your taṭayyur (the act of considering omens) ([Abu Hayyan said regarding this reading: "aṭṭayrukum" is a verbal noun of "aṭṭayara," in which the ta' was assimilated into the ṭa', so the hamzat al-wasl (connecting hamza) was introduced in the past tense and the verbal noun.]). "Even if you are reminded" (36:19): Qatadah said: even if you are reminded, you take omens. There are nine readings concerning it. The people of Medina read "ayna dhukkirtum" with the second hamza lightened. The people of Kufa read "a-in" with both hamzas made clear. The third mode: "a-a-in dhukkirtum" with two hamzas and an alif between them; the alif was introduced out of dislike of joining the two hamzas. The fourth mode: "ā-yn" with a hamza followed by an alif, and after the alif a lightened hamza. The fifth reading: "a-a-na" with two fatha-vowelled hamzas and an alif between them. The sixth mode: "a-a-na" with two clearly articulated fatha-vowelled hamzas. Al-Farra' related that this reading was that of Abu Razin.

I say: al-Tha'labi related it from Zirr ibn Hubaysh and Ibn al-Sumayq. 'Isa ibn 'Umar and al-Hasan al-Basri read: "Qalu ṭa'irukum ma'akum ayna dhukkirtum" with the meaning of "where" (ḥayth). Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa', al-Hasan, and Talhah read "dhukirtum" with lightening (takhfif). al-Nahhas mentioned all of this. al-Mahdawi related from Talhah ibn Musarrif and 'Isa al-Hamadhani: "a-n dhukkirtum" with the madd (prolongation), on the basis that the interrogative hamza entered upon a fatha-vowelled hamza. al-Majshun read: "an dhukkirtum" with one fatha-vowelled hamza. These are nine readings. Ibn Harmuz read "ṭayrukum ma'ak."

"Even if you are reminded" means: if you are admonished, you take omens. This is a resumptive statement, meaning: if you are admonished, you take omens. It was also said: they only took omens when it reached them that every prophet who called his people and was not answered, his end was destruction. Qatadah said: "Musrifun" (transgressing) means you are excessive in your taṭayyur. Yahya ibn Sallam said: excessive in your disbelief. Ibn Bahr said: "al-sarf" (excess) here means corruption, and its meaning is: rather, you are a people who corrupt. It was also said: "musrifun" means polytheists, and excess (isrāf) is going beyond the limit, and the polytheist goes beyond the limit.

He was Habib ibn Murri, and he was a carpenter (najjar). It is also said he was a cobbler (iskaf), and it is said he was a fuller (qassar). Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Muqatil said: he was Habib ibn Isra'il the carpenter, and he used to carve idols. He was among those who believed in the Prophet (ﷺ), and between them were six hundred years, just as Tubba' al-Akbar, Waraqah ibn Nawfal and others believed in him. No one believed in a prophet except after his emergence.

Wahb said: Habib had leprosy, and his dwelling was at the farthest of the gates of the city. For seventy years he devoted himself to worshipping idols, calling people to them, hoping they would have mercy on him and relieve his affliction, but they did not respond to him. When he saw the messengers, they invited him to worship God. He said: "Is there any sign?" They said: "Yes, we call upon our Lord, the All-Powerful, and He will relieve you of what afflicts you." He said: "This is strange to me. I have called upon these gods for seventy years to relieve me, and they could not do it. So how would your Lord relieve him in a single morning?" They said: "Yes, our Lord is capable of whatever He wills, and these [gods] benefit nothing and harm nothing." So he believed, and they prayed to their Lord, and God removed what was upon him, as though there had never been any affliction in him. Then he returned to earning his living, and when evening came he gave away his earnings: he fed his dependents half and gave half in charity.

When his people resolved to kill the messengers, he came to them. ﴿He said: "O my people, follow the messengers."﴾ Qatadah said: He had been worshipping God in a cave, and when he heard the news of the messengers he came running. He said to the messengers: "Do you ask a wage for what you have brought?" They said: "No, our reward is only with God." Abu al-'Aliyah said: So he was convinced of their truthfulness, believed in them, and turned to his people and said: ﴿"O my people, follow the messengers."﴾ That is, if they were accused of falsehood, they would have asked you for money. ﴿"And they are rightly guided,"﴾ so follow their guidance.

﴿"And why should I not worship He who created me?"﴾ Qatadah said: His people said to him: "Are you on their religion?!" So he said: ﴿"And why should I not worship He who created me?"﴾ that is, who brought me into being. ﴿"And to Him you will be returned."﴾ This is an argument from him against them. He attributed the creation to himself, because it is a blessing upon him that requires gratitude; and the return he attributed to them, because it is a warning that requires restraint. So attributing the blessing to himself was a more evident expression of gratitude, and attributing the return to the disbelievers was more forceful in effect.

﴿"Shall I take besides Him gods?"﴾ meaning idols. ﴿"If the Most Merciful wills harm for me,"﴾ meaning the sickness that had afflicted him. ﴿"Their intercession will avail me nothing, nor can they rescue me,"﴾ that is, deliver me from the affliction I am in. ﴿"Indeed, I would then be in manifest error,"﴾ meaning if I did that. That is, manifest loss. ﴿"Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so hear me."﴾ Ibn Mas'ud said: He addressed the messengers by saying that he believes in God, their Lord. The meaning of ﴿"so hear me"﴾ is "so bear witness," that is, be witnesses for me to my faith. Ka'b and Wahb said: He said that to his people: "Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, whom you have disbelieved in."

It is also said that when he said to his people ﴿"Follow the messengers. Follow those who ask you no reward"﴾ they took him to the king and said: "You have followed our enemy." He prolonged his speech with them in order to occupy them with that, away from killing the messengers, until he said: ﴿"Indeed, I have believed in your Lord,"﴾ whereupon they pounced on him and killed him. Ibn Mas'ud said: They trampled him with their feet until his intestine (qasab) [[the qasab is the intestine]] came out from his rear, and he was thrown into a well, which is the Rass, and they are the people of the Rass. In another report, they killed the three messengers. Al-Suddi said: They stoned him while he was saying: "O God, guide my people," until they killed him. Al-Kalbi said: They dug a pit, put him in it, and covered him over with earth, so he died by being buried. Al-Hasan said: They burned him, and hung him from the wall of the city; his grave is in the wall of Antioch, as related by al-Tha'labi. Al-Qushayri said: Al-Hasan said: when the people wanted to kill him, God raised him to the heaven, and he is in Paradise, not dying until the sky perishes and Paradise is destroyed; when God restores Paradise, he will be admitted into it. It is also said: they sawed him with a saw until it came out between his legs, and by God his soul did not leave except to Paradise, and he entered it. That is the meaning of His words: ﴿"It was said: Enter Paradise."﴾ A group said: the meaning of ﴿"It was said: Enter Paradise"﴾ is that Paradise was made obligatory for you, so this is a report that he had merited entry into Paradise, since entry into it is merited after the Resurrection.

I say: The apparent meaning of the verse is that when he was killed, it was said to him: ﴿"Enter Paradise."﴾ Qatadah said: God admitted him into Paradise, and he is there alive and provided for, intending the words of the Exalted: ﴿"And do not think of those who have been killed in the way of God as dead; rather, they are alive with their Lord, being provided for."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 169], as its explanation has preceded in Al 'Imran [[see vol. 4, p. 268 onward, first or second edition]]. And God knows best.

His words, exalted be He: ﴿"He said: 'Would that my people knew,"﴾ are arranged upon the supposition of a questioner asking what was said at that great success, which is "by what my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honored." It is read ﴿"among the honored"﴾ [variant reading]. Regarding the meaning of his wish there are two opinions. The first: he wished that they would know his condition, so that they would know the goodness of his destination and the praiseworthiness of his end. The second: he wished that for them so that they would believe as he believed and arrive at a state like his.

Ibn 'Abbas said: He advised his people while alive and dead. Al-Qushayri traced it to the Prophet: in a report, he (peace be upon him) said concerning this verse: "He gave them counsel during his life and after his death." Ibn Abi Layla said: The foremost of the nations are three who never disbelieved in God for the blink of an eye: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who is the best of them; the believer of the family of Pharaoh; and the companion of Ya Sin. They are the truthful (siddiqun). Al-Zamakhshari mentioned it as a report traced to the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

In this verse there is a great admonition and an indication of the obligation to restrain anger, to be forbearing toward the ignorant, to show compassion toward one who has thrown himself into the midst of the wicked and the transgressors, to exert oneself in rescuing him, to be gentle in ransoming him, and to occupy oneself with that rather than gloating over him or invoking evil upon him. Do you not see how he wished good for his killers, and for those who sought to harm him, while they were disbelievers worshipping idols? When Habib was killed, God was angry on his behalf and hastened vengeance upon his people. He commanded Gabriel, who shouted at them with one cry, and they all died to the last one. That is His saying: ﴿"And We did not send down upon his people after him any host from the heaven, nor were We ever to send [one]."﴾ That is, We did not send down upon them any message or prophet after his killing. Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Hasan said so. Al-Hasan said: "The host" means the angels who descend with revelation upon the prophets. It is also said: "The host" means armies, that is, I did not need to send hosts or armies to destroy them, but I destroyed them with a single cry. Ibn Mas'ud and others said this. So His saying ﴿"nor were We ever to send [one]"﴾ belittles their matter, meaning: We destroyed them with a single cry after that man, or after his being raised to the heaven. It is also said: ﴿"nor were We ever to send [one]"﴾ against those who came before them.

Al-Zamakhshari: If you ask, why did He send hosts from the heaven on the day of Badr and the Trench? He said: ﴿"So We sent upon them a wind and hosts you did not see"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 9], and He said: ﴿"with three thousand angels sent down"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 124], and ﴿"with five thousand angels marked"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 125]. I say: One angel would have sufficed, for the cities of the people of Lot were destroyed by a feather from the wing of Gabriel, and the lands of Thamud and the people of Salih by a cry; but God preferred Muhammad (ﷺ) in every respect over all the prophets and the steadfast messengers, let alone Habib the carpenter, and He granted him from the causes of honor and exaltation what He granted to no one else. Among that is that He sent down hosts for him from the heaven. It is as if His saying ﴿"We did not send down"﴾ and ﴿"nor were We ever to send [one]"﴾ indicated that sending down hosts is among the great matters for which none is fit except one like you, and that We would not do it for anyone else.

﴿"It was not but one cry"﴾: the common reading is "wahidatan" with a fatha, on the presumption that their punishment was nothing but one cry. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa', Shaybah and al-A'raj read "sayhatun" with a damma here, and in His saying ﴿"It was not but one cry, and at once they were all extinguished"﴾; they made the verb "kana" mean "to occur" or "to happen," as if he said: nothing befell them except one cry. Abu Hatim and many grammarians rejected this reading because of the feminine form, and held it to be weak, just as "ma qamat illa Hind" would be weak, since the meaning would be "no one stood except Hind." Abu Hatim said: If it were as Abu Ja'far read, it would say "in kana illa sayhatun." Al-Nahhas said: Nothing of this is impossible. One says: "ma ja'atni illa jariyatuka," meaning "no woman or slave-girl came to me except your slave-girl." The estimate in the reading with the damma is what Abu Ishaq said: he said the meaning is: "if there was upon them any cry except one cry," and others estimated it: "nothing befell them except one cry." And "kana" in the sense of "waqa'a" is frequent in Arabic speech. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Aswad read—and it is said that it is so in the codex of 'Abdullah—"in kanat illa zaqatan wahidhah," but this contradicts the Mushaf. Moreover, the well-known form is "zaqa yazqu" when one cries out, and from it the proverb "heavier than the zawaqi" (the cries). On this basis it should have been "ziqwah." Al-Nahhas mentioned this.

I say: Al-Jawhari said: "al-zaqw" and "al-zaqy" are verbal nouns; "al-sada" (the echo) "yazqu zuqa'an," that is, it cried out, and every crier is "zaqin," and "al-ziqyah" is the cry. I say: On this basis one may say "zaqwah" and "zaqyah" are two dialects, so the readings are sound and there is no objection to them. And God knows best. ﴿"And at once they were extinguished,"﴾ that is, dead, still, like extinguished ashes. Qatadah said: destroyed. The meaning is the same.

He was Habib ibn Murri, and he was a carpenter (najjar). It is also said he was a cobbler (iskaf), and it is said he was a fuller (qassar). Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Muqatil said: he was Habib ibn Isra'il the carpenter, and he used to carve idols. He was among those who believed in the Prophet (ﷺ), and between them were six hundred years, just as Tubba' al-Akbar, Waraqah ibn Nawfal and others believed in him. No one believed in a prophet except after his emergence.

Wahb said: Habib had leprosy, and his dwelling was at the farthest of the gates of the city. For seventy years he devoted himself to worshipping idols, calling people to them, hoping they would have mercy on him and relieve his affliction, but they did not respond to him. When he saw the messengers, they invited him to worship God. He said: "Is there any sign?" They said: "Yes, we call upon our Lord, the All-Powerful, and He will relieve you of what afflicts you." He said: "This is strange to me. I have called upon these gods for seventy years to relieve me, and they could not do it. So how would your Lord relieve him in a single morning?" They said: "Yes, our Lord is capable of whatever He wills, and these [gods] benefit nothing and harm nothing." So he believed, and they prayed to their Lord, and God removed what was upon him, as though there had never been any affliction in him. Then he returned to earning his living, and when evening came he gave away his earnings: he fed his dependents half and gave half in charity.

When his people resolved to kill the messengers, he came to them. ﴿He said: "O my people, follow the messengers."﴾ Qatadah said: He had been worshipping God in a cave, and when he heard the news of the messengers he came running. He said to the messengers: "Do you ask a wage for what you have brought?" They said: "No, our reward is only with God." Abu al-'Aliyah said: So he was convinced of their truthfulness, believed in them, and turned to his people and said: ﴿"O my people, follow the messengers."﴾ That is, if they were accused of falsehood, they would have asked you for money. ﴿"And they are rightly guided,"﴾ so follow their guidance.

﴿"And why should I not worship He who created me?"﴾ Qatadah said: His people said to him: "Are you on their religion?!" So he said: ﴿"And why should I not worship He who created me?"﴾ that is, who brought me into being. ﴿"And to Him you will be returned."﴾ This is an argument from him against them. He attributed the creation to himself, because it is a blessing upon him that requires gratitude; and the return he attributed to them, because it is a warning that requires restraint. So attributing the blessing to himself was a more evident expression of gratitude, and attributing the return to the disbelievers was more forceful in effect.

﴿"Shall I take besides Him gods?"﴾ meaning idols. ﴿"If the Most Merciful wills harm for me,"﴾ meaning the sickness that had afflicted him. ﴿"Their intercession will avail me nothing, nor can they rescue me,"﴾ that is, deliver me from the affliction I am in. ﴿"Indeed, I would then be in manifest error,"﴾ meaning if I did that. That is, manifest loss. ﴿"Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so hear me."﴾ Ibn Mas'ud said: He addressed the messengers by saying that he believes in God, their Lord. The meaning of ﴿"so hear me"﴾ is "so bear witness," that is, be witnesses for me to my faith. Ka'b and Wahb said: He said that to his people: "Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, whom you have disbelieved in."

It is also said that when he said to his people ﴿"Follow the messengers. Follow those who ask you no reward"﴾ they took him to the king and said: "You have followed our enemy." He prolonged his speech with them in order to occupy them with that, away from killing the messengers, until he said: ﴿"Indeed, I have believed in your Lord,"﴾ whereupon they pounced on him and killed him. Ibn Mas'ud said: They trampled him with their feet until his intestine (qasab) [[the qasab is the intestine]] came out from his rear, and he was thrown into a well, which is the Rass, and they are the people of the Rass. In another report, they killed the three messengers. Al-Suddi said: They stoned him while he was saying: "O God, guide my people," until they killed him. Al-Kalbi said: They dug a pit, put him in it, and covered him over with earth, so he died by being buried. Al-Hasan said: They burned him, and hung him from the wall of the city; his grave is in the wall of Antioch, as related by al-Tha'labi. Al-Qushayri said: Al-Hasan said: when the people wanted to kill him, God raised him to the heaven, and he is in Paradise, not dying until the sky perishes and Paradise is destroyed; when God restores Paradise, he will be admitted into it. It is also said: they sawed him with a saw until it came out between his legs, and by God his soul did not leave except to Paradise, and he entered it. That is the meaning of His words: ﴿"It was said: Enter Paradise."﴾ A group said: the meaning of ﴿"It was said: Enter Paradise"﴾ is that Paradise was made obligatory for you, so this is a report that he had merited entry into Paradise, since entry into it is merited after the Resurrection.

I say: The apparent meaning of the verse is that when he was killed, it was said to him: ﴿"Enter Paradise."﴾ Qatadah said: God admitted him into Paradise, and he is there alive and provided for, intending the words of the Exalted: ﴿"And do not think of those who have been killed in the way of God as dead; rather, they are alive with their Lord, being provided for."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 169], as its explanation has preceded in Al 'Imran [[see vol. 4, p. 268 onward, first or second edition]]. And God knows best.

His words, exalted be He: ﴿"He said: 'Would that my people knew,"﴾ are arranged upon the supposition of a questioner asking what was said at that great success, which is "by what my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honored." It is read ﴿"among the honored"﴾ [variant reading]. Regarding the meaning of his wish there are two opinions. The first: he wished that they would know his condition, so that they would know the goodness of his destination and the praiseworthiness of his end. For seventy years he devoted himself to worshipping idols, calling people to them, hoping they would have mercy on him and relieve his affliction, but they did not respond to him. When he saw the messengers, they invited him to worship God. He said: "Is there any sign?" They said: "Yes, we call upon our Lord, the All-Powerful, and He will relieve you of what afflicts you." He said: "This is strange to me. I have called upon these gods for seventy years to relieve me, and they could not do it. So how would your Lord relieve him in a single morning?" They said: "Yes, our Lord is capable of whatever He wills, and these [gods] benefit nothing and harm nothing." So he believed, and they prayed to their Lord, and God removed what was upon him, as though there had never been any affliction in him. Then he returned to earning his living, and when evening came he gave away his earnings: he fed his dependents half and gave half in charity.

When his people resolved to kill the messengers, he came to them. ﴿He said: "O my people, follow the messengers."﴾ Qatadah said: He had been worshipping God in a cave, and when he heard the news of the messengers he came running. He said to the messengers: "Do you ask a wage for what you have brought?" They said: "No, our reward is only with God." Abu al-'Aliyah said: So he was convinced of their truthfulness, believed in them, and turned to his people and said: ﴿"O my people, follow the messengers."﴾ That is, if they were accused of falsehood, they would have asked you for money. ﴿"And they are rightly guided,"﴾ so follow their guidance.

﴿"And why should I not worship He who created me?"﴾ Qatadah said: His people said to him: "Are you on their religion?!" So he said: ﴿"And why should I not worship He who created me?"﴾ that is, who brought me into being. ﴿"And to Him you will be returned."﴾ This is an argument from him against them. He attributed the creation to himself, because it is a blessing upon him that requires gratitude; and the return he attributed to them, because it is a warning that requires restraint. So attributing the blessing to himself was a more evident expression of gratitude, and attributing the return to the disbelievers was more forceful in effect.

﴿"Shall I take besides Him gods?"﴾ meaning idols. ﴿"If the Most Merciful wills harm for me,"﴾ meaning the sickness that had afflicted him. ﴿"Their intercession will avail me nothing, nor can they rescue me,"﴾ that is, deliver me from the affliction I am in. ﴿"Indeed, I would then be in manifest error,"﴾ meaning if I did that. That is, manifest loss. ﴿"Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so hear me."﴾ Ibn Mas'ud said: He addressed the messengers by saying that he believes in God, their Lord. The meaning of ﴿"so hear me"﴾ is "so bear witness," that is, be witnesses for me to my faith. Ka'b and Wahb said: He said that to his people: "Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, whom you have disbelieved in."

It is also said that when he said to his people ﴿"Follow the messengers. Follow those who ask you no reward"﴾ they took him to the king and said: "You have followed our enemy." He prolonged his speech with them in order to occupy them with that, away from killing the messengers, until he said: ﴿"Indeed, I have believed in your Lord,"﴾ whereupon they pounced on him and killed him. Ibn Mas'ud said: They trampled him with their feet until his intestine (qasab) [[the qasab is the intestine]] came out from his rear, and he was thrown into a well, which is the Rass, and they are the people of the Rass. In another report, they killed the three messengers. Al-Suddi said: They stoned him while he was saying: "O God, guide my people," until they killed him. Al-Kalbi said: They dug a pit, put him in it, and covered him over with earth, so he died by being buried. Al-Hasan said: They burned him, and hung him from the wall of the city; his grave is in the wall of Antioch, as related by al-Tha'labi. Al-Qushayri said: Al-Hasan said: when the people wanted to kill him, God raised him to the heaven, and he is in Paradise, not dying until the sky perishes and Paradise is destroyed; when God restores Paradise, he will be admitted into it. It is also said: they sawed him with a saw until it came out between his legs, and by God his soul did not leave except to Paradise, and he entered it. That is the meaning of His words: ﴿"It was said: Enter Paradise."﴾ A group said: the meaning of ﴿"It was said: Enter Paradise"﴾ is that Paradise was made obligatory for you, so this is a report that he had merited entry into Paradise, since entry into it is merited after the Resurrection.

I say: The apparent meaning of the verse is that when he was killed, it was said to him: ﴿"Enter Paradise."﴾ Qatadah said: God admitted him into Paradise, and he is there alive and provided for, intending the words of the Exalted: ﴿"And do not think of those who have been killed in the way of God as dead; rather, they are alive with their Lord, being provided for."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 169], as its explanation has preceded in Al 'Imran [[see vol. 4, p. 268 onward, first or second edition]]. And God knows best.

His words, exalted be He: ﴿"He said: 'Would that my people knew,"﴾ are arranged upon the supposition of a questioner asking what was said at that great success, which is "by what my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honored." It is read ﴿"among the honored"﴾ [variant reading]. Regarding the meaning of his wish there are two opinions. The first: he wished that they would know his condition, so that they would know the goodness of his destination and the praiseworthiness of his end. The second: he wished that for them so that they would believe as he believed and arrive at a state like his.

Ibn 'Abbas said: He advised his people while alive and dead. Al-Qushayri traced it to the Prophet: in a report, he (peace be upon him) said concerning this verse: "He gave them counsel during his life and after his death." Ibn Abi Layla said: The foremost of the nations are three who never disbelieved in God for the blink of an eye: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who is the best of them; the believer of the family of Pharaoh; and the companion of Ya Sin. They are the truthful (siddiqun). Al-Zamakhshari mentioned it as a report traced to the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

In this verse there is a great admonition and an indication of the obligation to restrain anger, to be forbearing toward the ignorant, to show compassion toward one who has thrown himself into the midst of the wicked and the transgressors, to exert oneself in rescuing him, to be gentle in ransoming him, and to occupy oneself with that rather than gloating over him or invoking evil upon him. Do you not see how he wished good for his killers, and for those who sought to harm him, while they were disbelievers worshipping idols? When Habib was killed, God was angry on his behalf and hastened vengeance upon his people. He commanded Gabriel, who shouted at them with one cry, and they all died to the last one. That is His saying: ﴿"And We did not send down upon his people after him any host from the heaven, nor were We ever to send [one]."﴾ That is, We did not send down upon them any message or prophet after his killing. Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Hasan said so. Al-Hasan said: "The host" means the angels who descend with revelation upon the prophets. It is also said: "The host" means armies, that is, I did not need to send hosts or armies to destroy them, but I destroyed them with a single cry. Ibn Mas'ud and others said this. So His saying ﴿"nor were We ever to send [one]"﴾ belittles their matter, meaning: We destroyed them with a single cry after that man, or after his being raised to the heaven. It is also said: ﴿"nor were We ever to send [one]"﴾ against those who came before them.

Al-Zamakhshari: If you ask, why did He send hosts from the heaven on the day of Badr and the Trench? He said: ﴿"So We sent upon them a wind and hosts you did not see"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 9], and He said: ﴿"with three thousand angels sent down"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 124], and ﴿"with five thousand angels marked"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 125]. I say: One angel would have sufficed, for the cities of the people of Lot were destroyed by a feather from the wing of Gabriel, and the lands of Thamud and the people of Salih by a cry; but God preferred Muhammad (ﷺ) in every respect over all the prophets and the steadfast messengers, let alone Habib the carpenter, and He granted him from the causes of honor and exaltation what He granted to no one else. Among that is that He sent down hosts for him from the heaven. It is as if His saying ﴿"We did not send down"﴾ and ﴿"nor were We ever to send [one]"﴾ indicated that sending down hosts is among the great matters for which none is fit except one like you, and that We would not do it for anyone else.

﴿"It was not but one cry"﴾: the common reading is "wahidatan" with a fatha, on the presumption that their punishment was nothing but one cry. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa', Shaybah and al-A'raj read "sayhatun" with a damma here, and in His saying ﴿"It was not but one cry, and at once they were all extinguished"﴾; they made the verb "kana" mean "to occur" or "to happen," as if he said: nothing befell them except one cry. Abu Hatim and many grammarians rejected this reading because of the feminine form, and held it to be weak, just as "ma qamat illa Hind" would be weak, since the meaning would be "no one stood except Hind." Abu Hatim said: If it were as Abu Ja'far read, it would say "in kana illa sayhatun." Al-Nahhas said: Nothing of this is impossible. One says: "ma ja'atni illa jariyatuka," meaning "no woman or slave-girl came to me except your slave-girl." The estimate in the reading with the damma is what Abu Ishaq said: he said the meaning is: "if there was upon them any cry except one cry," and others estimated it: "nothing befell them except one cry." And "kana" in the sense of "waqa'a" is frequent in Arabic speech. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Aswad read—and it is said that it is so in the codex of 'Abdullah—"in kanat illa zaqatan wahidhah," but this contradicts the Mushaf. Moreover, the well-known form is "zaqa yazqu" when one cries out, and from it the proverb "heavier than the zawaqi" (the cries). On this basis it should have been "ziqwah." Al-Nahhas mentioned this.

I say: Al-Jawhari said: "al-zaqw" and "al-zaqy" are verbal nouns; "al-sada" (the echo) "yazqu zuqa'an," that is, it cried out, and every crier is "zaqin," and "al-ziqyah" is the cry. I say: On this basis one may say "zaqwah" and "zaqyah" are two dialects, so the readings are sound and there is no objection to them. And God knows best. ﴿"And at once they were extinguished,"﴾ that is, dead, still, like extinguished ashes. Qatadah said: destroyed. The meaning is the same.

**Allah the Exalted said: "Alas for the servants!"** (﴿يا حَسْرَةً عَلَى الْعِبادِ﴾). *Hasratan* is in the accusative case because it is a vocative of an indefinite noun (*nida' nakira*, the address of an unspecified noun). According to the Basran grammarians, no case other than the accusative is permissible here.

In the reading of Ubayy, it is *"Ya hasrata al-'ibad"* in the construct form (*idafa*).

Linguistically, *hasra* (regret) means that a person is overtaken by remorse to the point that he becomes exhausted (*hasir*).

Al-Farra' claimed that the preferred reading is the accusative, but that it would also be correct to put the indefinite noun in the nominative when it is followed by a relative clause (*sila*). He cited several examples, including that he heard from the Arabs: *"Ya muhtamman bi-amrina la tahtamma"* ("O you who are concerned with our affair, do not be concerned"). He also recited:

*"Ya dara ghayyaraha al-bila taghyira"*
("O abode, decay has altered you greatly")
[The line is by al-Ahwas, and its completion is: *"Wa-safat 'alayha al-rihu ba'daka mawwara"* ("And the wind has swept over it after you, carrying dust").]

Al-Nahhas said: In this view there is an annulment of the chapter of the vocative, or most of it, because it would make the pure indefinite noun nominative, make what is equivalent to a construct phrase nominative in a long construction, delete the tanwin (nunation) medially, and make nominative what is in meaning an object, without any cause requiring it. As for what al-Farra' reported from the Arabs, it does not resemble what he permitted, because the underlying form of *"Ya muhtamman bi-amrina la tahtamma"* is with inversion and deletion of the words, and the meaning is *"Ya ayyuha al-muhtammu la tahtamma bi-amrina"* ("O you who are concerned, do not be concerned with our affair"). The underlying form of the line is: *"Ya ayyatuha al-dar"* ("O abode"), and then the address was shifted, meaning: *"Ya ha'ula'i, ghayyara hadhihi al-dara al-bila"* ("O people, decay has altered this abode"), just as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿حَتَّى إِذا كُنْتُمْ فِي الْفُلْكِ وَجَرَيْنَ بِهِمْ﴾ ("Until when you are in the ship and they sail with them", Yunus 22). So *"hasratan"* is in the accusative as a vocative, just as you say, "O man, come forward," and the meaning of this address is the place where regret is present.

Al-Tabari said: The meaning is: "O regret from the servants over themselves, and remorse and anguish at their mockery of the messengers, peace be upon them."

Ibn 'Abbas said: *"Ya hasratan 'ala al-'ibad"* means "Alas for the servants" (*ya wayla 'ala al-'ibad*). And from him also: these people have been placed in the position of those for whom one feels regret.

Al-Rabi' reported from Anas, from Abu al-'Aliya, that "the servants" here refers to the messengers. That is because when the disbelievers saw the punishment, they said: ﴿يا حَسْرَةً عَلَى الْعِبادِ﴾, regretting their killing of them and their abandonment of belief in them, so they wished for belief when belief no longer benefited them. Mujahid also said this.

Al-Dahhak said: it is the regret of the angels over the disbelievers when they denied the messengers.

It has also been said that ﴿يا حَسْرَةً عَلَى الْعِبادِ﴾ is the statement of the man who came from the farthest part of the city, running (Ya-Sin 20), when the people rushed to kill him.

It has also been said that the three messengers were the ones who said, when the people killed that man who had come from the farthest part of the city running, and the punishment befell the people: "Alas for these people!" as if they feared that they might have believed.

It has also been said that this is the statement of the people, who said when they killed the man and the messengers departed from them, or when they killed the man along with the three messengers, according to the differing narrations: "Alas for these messengers and for this man! Would that we had believed in them at the time when belief benefits!" The speech is complete at this point, and then it begins anew with: ﴿ما يَأْتِيهِمْ مِنْ رَسُولٍ﴾ ("No messenger comes to them", Ya-Sin 30).

Ibn Hurmuz, Muslim ibn Jundab and 'Ikrima read *"Ya hasrah 'ala al-'ibad"* with the *ha'* pronounced with a sukun (silent), out of eagerness for clarity and for fixing the meaning in the soul, since it is a place of admonition and warning, and the Arabs do this in such contexts even when it is not a place of pause. Among this is what is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he would pause in his recitation letter by letter, out of eagerness for clarity and comprehension.

It is permissible for *"'ala al-'ibad"* to be connected to *hasrah* (regret). It is also permissible for it to be connected to something elided, not to *hasrah*. It is as if he intended a pause at *hasrah*, making the *ha'* silent, and then said: *"'ala al-'ibad"*, meaning: "I feel regret over the servants."

From Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and others: *"Ya hasrata al-'ibad"* is a construct phrase with "'ala" elided. This is contrary to the Mushaf.

It is permissible for it to be an idafa to the agent, so that *al-'ibad* would be the doers, as if when they witnessed the punishment they regretted, and this is like your saying: *"Ya qiyama Zayd"* ("O standing of Zayd"). It is also permissible for it to be an idafa to the object, so that *al-'ibad* would be the objects, as if the servants were regretted by one who feels compassion for them. The reading of one who reads *"Ya hasratan 'ala al-'ibad"* strengthens this meaning.

Sibawayh said: *"Anna"* (in ﴿أَنَّهُمْ إِلَيْهِمْ لَا يَرْجِعُونَ﴾) is a substitute for *"kam"* (how many), and the meaning of *kam* here is informative (not interrogative), which is why what is not an interrogative may be substituted for it. The meaning is: "Did they not see that the generations whom We destroyed, that they do not return to them?"

Al-Farra' said: *"Kam"* is in the accusative position in two respects. The first is governed by *"yaraw"* (they saw), and he cited as evidence that in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is: *"Alam yaraw man ahlakna"* ("Did they not see whom We destroyed"). The second is that *"kam"* is in the accusative position governed by *"ahlakna"* (We destroyed).

Al-Nahhas said: The first opinion is impossible, because *"kam"* is not governed by what precedes it, since it is an interrogative, and it is impossible for an interrogative to enter into the predicate of what precedes it. The same applies when it is informative. Although Sibawayh had alluded to some of this when he made *"annahum"* a substitute for *"kam"*, Muhammad ibn Yazid (al-Mubarrad) rejected that most strongly and said: *"Kam"* is in the accusative position governed by *"ahlakna"*, and *"annahum"* is in the accusative position, and the meaning according to him with *"bi-annahum"* is: "Did they not see how many generations We destroyed before them by extermination?" He said: The evidence for this is that in the reading of 'Abdullah it is: *"Man ahlakna qablahum mina al-qurun annahum ilayhim la yarji'un"*.

Al-Hasan read *"Innahum ilayhim la yarji'un"* with a kasra on the hamza, as a resumption (*isti'naf*, a new sentence). This verse is a refutation of the one who claims that some of the creation return before the Resurrection after death, meaning on the Day of Resurrection for the recompense.

Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Hamza read *"Wa-in kullun lamma"* with the *lamma* having a shadda (doubled consonant). The others read it without the shadda. *"In"* here is the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, and what follows it is nominative as the subject, and what follows that is the predicate. Its operation has been nullified because its form has changed, and the *lam* has been retained in the predicate to distinguish it from *in* meaning *ma* (not).

According to Abu 'Ubayda, *"ma"* is superfluous. The implied meaning for him is: "Indeed each one is surely all gathered (*lajami'un*)."

Al-Farra' said: Whoever reads with the shadda makes *"lamma"* mean *"illa"* (except), and *"in"* means *"ma"* (not), meaning: "Not all except that they are gathered," like His saying: ﴿إِنْ هُوَ إِلَّا رَجُلٌ بِهِ جِنَّةٌ﴾ ("He is not but a man in whom there is madness", al-Mu'minun 25).

Sibawayh related the expression in the saying: "I ask you by Allah, *lamma* (except that) you did it," and al-Kisa'i claimed that this is not known. This meaning has already passed in [Hud]. [See vol. 9, p. 105 and following, first or second edition.]

In the reading of Ubayy it is: *"Wa-in minhum illa jami'un ladayna muhdarun"* ("And there is not among them anyone except that all are present before Us").

Al-Farra' said: Whoever reads with the shadda makes *"lamma"* mean *"illa"* (except), and *"in"* means *"ma"* (not), meaning: "Not all except that they are gathered," like His saying: ﴿إِنْ هُوَ إِلَّا رَجُلٌ بِهِ جِنَّةٌ﴾ ("He is not but a man in whom there is madness", al-Mu'minun 25).

Sibawayh related the expression in the saying: "I ask you by Allah, *lamma* (except that) you did it," and al-Kisa'i claimed that this is not known. This meaning has already passed in [Hud]. [See vol. 9, p. 105 and following, first or second edition.]

In the reading of Ubayy it is: *"Wa-in minhum illa jami'un ladayna muhdarun"* ("And there is not among them anyone except that all are present before Us").

**Allah the Exalted said: "Alas for the servants!"** (﴿يا حَسْرَةً عَلَى الْعِبادِ﴾). *Hasratan* is in the accusative case because it is a vocative of an indefinite noun (*nida' nakira*, the address of an unspecified noun). According to the Basran grammarians, no case other than the accusative is permissible here.

In the reading of Ubayy, it is *"Ya hasrata al-'ibad"* in the construct form (*idafa*).

Linguistically, *hasra* (regret) means that a person is overtaken by remorse to the point that he becomes exhausted (*hasir*).

Al-Farra' claimed that the preferred reading is the accusative, but that it would also be correct to put the indefinite noun in the nominative when it is followed by a relative clause (*sila*). He cited several examples, including that he heard from the Arabs: *"Ya muhtamman bi-amrina la tahtamma"* ("O you who are concerned with our affair, do not be concerned"). He also recited:

*"Ya dara ghayyaraha al-bila taghyira"*
("O abode, decay has altered you greatly")
[The line is by al-Ahwas, and its completion is: *"Wa-safat 'alayha al-rihu ba'daka mawwara"* ("And the wind has swept over it after you, carrying dust").]

Al-Nahhas said: In this view there is an annulment of the chapter of the vocative, or most of it, because it would make the pure indefinite noun nominative, make what is equivalent to a construct phrase nominative in a long construction, delete the tanwin (nunation) medially, and make nominative what is in meaning an object, without any cause requiring it. As for what al-Farra' reported from the Arabs, it does not resemble what he permitted, because the underlying form of *"Ya muhtamman bi-amrina la tahtamma"* is with inversion and deletion of the words, and the meaning is *"Ya ayyuha al-muhtammu la tahtamma bi-amrina"* ("O you who are concerned, do not be concerned with our affair"). The underlying form of the line is: *"Ya ayyatuha al-dar"* ("O abode"), and then the address was shifted, meaning: *"Ya ha'ula'i, ghayyara hadhihi al-dara al-bila"* ("O people, decay has altered this abode"), just as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿حَتَّى إِذا كُنْتُمْ فِي الْفُلْكِ وَجَرَيْنَ بِهِمْ﴾ ("Until when you are in the ship and they sail with them", Yunus 22). So *"hasratan"* is in the accusative as a vocative, just as you say, "O man, come forward," and the meaning of this address is the place where regret is present.

Al-Tabari said: The meaning is: "O regret from the servants over themselves, and remorse and anguish at their mockery of the messengers, peace be upon them."

Ibn 'Abbas said: *"Ya hasratan 'ala al-'ibad"* means "Alas for the servants" (*ya wayla 'ala al-'ibad*). And from him also: these people have been placed in the position of those for whom one feels regret.

Al-Rabi' reported from Anas, from Abu al-'Aliya, that "the servants" here refers to the messengers. That is because when the disbelievers saw the punishment, they said: ﴿يا حَسْرَةً عَلَى الْعِبادِ﴾, regretting their killing of them and their abandonment of belief in them, so they wished for belief when belief no longer benefited them. Mujahid also said this.

Al-Dahhak said: it is the regret of the angels over the disbelievers when they denied the messengers.

It has also been said that ﴿يا حَسْرَةً عَلَى الْعِبادِ﴾ is the statement of the man who came from the farthest part of the city, running (Ya-Sin 20), when the people rushed to kill him.

It has also been said that the three messengers were the ones who said, when the people killed that man who had come from the farthest part of the city running, and the punishment befell the people: "Alas for these people!" as if they feared that they might have believed.

It has also been said that this is the statement of the people, who said when they killed the man and the messengers departed from them, or when they killed the man along with the three messengers, according to the differing narrations: "Alas for these messengers and for this man! Would that we had believed in them at the time when belief benefits!" The speech is complete at this point, and then it begins anew with: ﴿ما يَأْتِيهِمْ مِنْ رَسُولٍ﴾ ("No messenger comes to them", Ya-Sin 30).

Ibn Hurmuz, Muslim ibn Jundab and 'Ikrima read *"Ya hasrah 'ala al-'ibad"* with the *ha'* pronounced with a sukun (silent), out of eagerness for clarity and for fixing the meaning in the soul, since it is a place of admonition and warning, and the Arabs do this in such contexts even when it is not a place of pause. Among this is what is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he would pause in his recitation letter by letter, out of eagerness for clarity and comprehension.

It is permissible for *"'ala al-'ibad"* to be connected to *hasrah* (regret). It is also permissible for it to be connected to something elided, not to *hasrah*. It is as if he intended a pause at *hasrah*, making the *ha'* silent, and then said: *"'ala al-'ibad"*, meaning: "I feel regret over the servants."

From Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and others: *"Ya hasrata al-'ibad"* is a construct phrase with "'ala" elided. This is contrary to the Mushaf.

It is permissible for it to be an idafa to the agent, so that *al-'ibad* would be the doers, as if when they witnessed the punishment they regretted, and this is like your saying: *"Ya qiyama Zayd"* ("O standing of Zayd"). It is also permissible for it to be an idafa to the object, so that *al-'ibad* would be the objects, as if the servants were regretted by one who feels compassion for them. The reading of one who reads *"Ya hasratan 'ala al-'ibad"* strengthens this meaning.

Sibawayh said: *"Anna"* (in ﴿أَنَّهُمْ إِلَيْهِمْ لَا يَرْجِعُونَ﴾) is a substitute for *"kam"* (how many), and the meaning of *kam* here is informative (not interrogative), which is why what is not an interrogative may be substituted for it. The meaning is: "Did they not see that the generations whom We destroyed, that they do not return to them?"

Al-Farra' said: *"Kam"* is in the accusative position in two respects. The first is governed by *"yaraw"* (they saw), and he cited as evidence that in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is: *"Alam yaraw man ahlakna"* ("Did they not see whom We destroyed"). The second is that *"kam"* is in the accusative position governed by *"ahlakna"* (We destroyed).

Al-Nahhas said: The first opinion is impossible, because *"kam"* is not governed by what precedes it, since it is an interrogative, and it is impossible for an interrogative to enter into the predicate of what precedes it. The same applies when it is informative. Although Sibawayh had alluded to some of this when he made *"annahum"* a substitute for *"kam"*, Muhammad ibn Yazid (al-Mubarrad) rejected that most strongly and said: *"Kam"* is in the accusative position governed by *"ahlakna"*, and *"annahum"* is in the accusative position, and the meaning according to him with *"bi-annahum"* is: "Did they not see how many generations We destroyed before them by extermination?" He said: The evidence for this is that in the reading of 'Abdullah it is: *"Man ahlakna qablahum mina al-qurun annahum ilayhim la yarji'un"*.

Al-Hasan read *"Innahum ilayhim la yarji'un"* with a kasra on the hamza, as a resumption (*isti'naf*, a new sentence). This verse is a refutation of the one who claims that some of the creation return before the Resurrection after death, meaning on the Day of Resurrection for the recompense.

Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Hamza read *"Wa-in kullun lamma"* with the *lamma* having a shadda (doubled consonant). The others read it without the shadda. *"In"* here is the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, and what follows it is nominative as the subject, and what follows that is the predicate. Its operation has been nullified because its form has changed, and the *lam* has been retained in the predicate to distinguish it from *in* meaning *ma* (not).

In the reading of Ubayy it is: *"Wa-in minhum illa jami'un ladayna muhdarun"* ("And there is not among them anyone except that all are present before Us").

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 33–36:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth; We have brought it to life﴾. By this, Allah draws their attention to the resurrection of the dead, and reminds them of His oneness and the perfection of His power. It is the dead earth that He brought to life by vegetation and by bringing forth grain from it. ﴿So from it they eat﴾, that is, from the grain, and by it they nourish themselves. The people of Madinah read "al-mayyitah" with a shadda (tashdid), while the rest read it without it; this has been discussed previously [[See vol. 2, p. 216 and following, second edition.]]. ﴿And We placed in it﴾, that is, in the earth, ﴿gardens﴾, that is, orchards, ﴿of date palms and grapevines﴾, and He singled out these two for mention because they are the most excellent of fruits. ﴿And We caused springs to gush forth in it﴾, that is, in the orchards. ﴿That they may eat of its fruit﴾: the pronoun in "thamarihi" (its fruit) refers to the water of the springs, because the fruit is included within it; this was said by al-Jurjani, al-Mahdawi and others. It was also said: the meaning is, that they may eat of the fruit of what We have mentioned, just as He said: ﴿And indeed, in cattle there is a lesson for you; We give you to drink from what is in their bellies﴾ [al-Nahl: 66]. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "min thumurihi" with a damma on the tha' and the mim; the rest read both with a fatha. It is also reported from al-A'mash that he read the tha' with a damma and the mim with sukun. The discussion of this has already passed in [al-An'am [[See vol. 7, p. 49 and following, first or second edition.]]]. ﴿Wa-ma﴾ is in the genitive position by coordination with "min thamarihi", meaning: and of what their hands have made. The Kufans read "wa-ma 'amilat" without a pronoun (ha'). The rest read "'amilathu" according to the original form without deletion. Deletion of the relative pronoun (silah) is also common in speech because the noun is long. It is also permissible for "ma" to be a negation with no grammatical position, so it needs no relative clause and no returning pronoun, meaning: and their hands did not make it, from the crops which Allah caused to grow for them. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and Muqatil. Others said: the meaning is "and of that which their hands have made", that is, of the fruits, of the varieties of sweets and foods, and of what they prepare from grains through processing, such as bread and the oil extracted from sesame and olives. It was also said: this refers to what people plant. This meaning was also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. ﴿Glory be to He who created all the pairs﴾: He exalted Himself above the saying of the disbelievers, since they worshipped other than Him despite what they saw of His favours and the signs of His power. It contains an implied command, that is: glorify Him and exalt Him above whatever is unfitting for Him. It was also said: there is in it the sense of wonder, that is, how strange it is that these people disbelieve despite what they witness of these signs; and whoever marvels at something says: "Subhan Allah." "Al-azwaj" means the kinds and the categories, so every pair is a category, because they differ in colours, tastes, shapes, and size and largeness; their difference is their pairing. Qatadah said: it means the male and the female.

﴿Of what the earth grows﴾, that is, of vegetation, because it has categories.

﴿And of themselves﴾, that is, He created offspring from them in pairs, males and females. And ﴿of what they do not know﴾, that is, of the categories of His creation on land and sea, in the heavens and the earth. Then it is possible that what He creates is unknown to humankind but known to the angels, and it is also possible that it is unknown to every created being. The basis of the argument in this verse is that since He alone creates, He should not be associated with anything in worship.

**Verse 37–38**

Allah's saying: ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip away from it the day, and behold, they are in darkness.﴾ That is, a sign and an indication of Allah's oneness, His power, and the necessity of His divinity.

*Al-salkh* (السلخ) means to strip off and pull out. It is said: "Allah stripped him of his religion" (سلخه الله من دينه). It is then used in the sense of extracting. The disappearance of light and the coming of darkness have been treated as being like the stripping of something and the appearance of what was stripped, so this is a metaphor (*isti'arah*). *Muzlimun* (مظلمون) means "those who have entered into darkness." It is said: "adhlamna" (أظلمنا), meaning we entered the darkness of the night; "adhharna" (أظهرنا), meaning we entered the time of midday (*zuhr*). Likewise "asbahna" (أصبحنا), "adhha naa" (أضحينا), and "amsayna" (أمسينا). It has been said that *minhu* (منه) means *ankhu* (عنه), and the meaning is: We strip away from it the light of the day. "Fa-idha hum muzlimun" means: they are in darkness, because the light of the day spreads through the air and illuminates it; when it departs from it, the air becomes dark.

Allah's saying: ﴿And the sun runs on to a resting place for it.﴾ It is permissible for its estimated construction to be: "And a sign for them is the sun." It is also permissible for *al-shams* (الشمس) to be in the nominative by the implied presence of a verb that the following word explains. It is also permissible for it to be nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), with *tajri* (تجري) in the position of the predicate, meaning "running."

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Dharr, who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: "And the sun runs on to a resting place for it." He said: "Its resting place is beneath the Throne."

Also in it (Sahih Muslim), from Abu Dharr, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said one day: "Do you know where this sun goes?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "Indeed it runs until it reaches its resting place beneath the Throne, and it falls down prostrating, and it remains like that until it is said to it: 'Rise up, return from where you came,' and it returns and rises at dawn from its place of rising. Then it runs until it reaches its resting place beneath the Throne, and it falls down prostrating, and it remains like that until it is said to it: 'Rise up, return from where you came,' and it returns and rises at dawn from its place of rising. Then it runs; people notice nothing unusual from it, until it reaches its resting place, that beneath the Throne. Then it is said to it: 'Rise up, rise at dawn from your setting place,' and it rises at dawn from its setting place." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do you know when that is? That is when ﴿no soul will benefit from its faith, if it had not believed before, or earned good through its faith﴾" [al-An'am: 158].

The wording of al-Bukhari, from Abu Dharr, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Abu Dharr when the sun set: "Do you know where it goes?" I said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "It goes until it prostrates beneath the Throne, and it asks permission, and permission is granted to it. It is about to prostrate, but its prostration is not accepted, and it asks permission, but permission is not granted to it. It is said to it: 'Return from where you came,' so it rises from its setting place. That is His saying: ﴿And the sun runs on to a resting place for it. That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing﴾."

The wording of al-Tirmidhi, from Abu Dharr, who said: I entered the mosque when the sun had set, and the Prophet (ﷺ) was sitting. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Abu Dharr, do you know where this goes?" I said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "It goes and asks permission to prostrate, and permission is granted to it, and it is as if it were said to it: 'Rise from where you came,' and it rises from its setting place." He said: Then he recited: "That is a resting place for it." He said: That is the reading of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud). Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: This is a hasan sahih hadith.

Ikrimah said: When the sun sets, it enters a sanctuary (*mihrab*) beneath the Throne, glorifying Allah until morning. When it rises in the morning, it asks its Lord to excuse it from coming out. The Lord says to it: "And why is that?" It says: "When I come out, I am worshipped besides You." The Lord, Blessed and Exalted, says: "Come out; there is no blame on you for that. I shall send Hell to them with seventy thousand angels leading it, until they cause them to enter it."

Al-Kalbi and others said: The meaning is that it runs toward its furthest stations in setting, then it returns to its nearest stations. So its *mustaqarr* (مستقرّ) is its reaching the point beyond which it does not go, but from which it returns, like a person who travels a distance until he reaches the farthest point of his aim, fulfills his need, and then returns to the first dwelling from which he began his journey. This refers to the sun reaching its farthest station, which is its resting place when *al-han'ah* (الهنعة, a star) rises. That is the longest day of the year and that is the shortest night. The day is then fifteen hours and the night nine hours. Then it begins to decrease and the sun returns. When the Pleiades (*al-Thurayya*) rise, night and day are equal, each twelve hours. Then it reaches its nearest station, and *al-na'a'im* (النعائم, a group of stars) rise. That day is the shortest day, and the night is fifteen hours. Until the rising of the later *fargh al-dalw* (فرغ الدلو المؤخر, a star-station), night and day become equal. So the night takes from the day each day a tenth of a third of an hour, and every ten days a third of an hour, and every month a full hour, until they become equal, and the night takes until it reaches fifteen hours, and the day takes from the night likewise.

Al-Hasan said: For the sun in the year there are three hundred and sixty risings (*matli'*). It descends to a different rising every day, and then it does not descend to it again until the year is complete. So it runs through those stations, and they are its resting place. This is the same meaning as the previous one.

Ibn Abbas said: When it sets and reaches the point beyond which it does not go, it remains beneath the Throne until it rises.

I (al-Qurtubi) say: What Ibn Abbas said gathers the opinions, so consider it carefully. It has also been said: its resting place is until the end of its term at the end of the world.

Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas read: ﴿And the sun runs, there is no resting place for it,﴾ meaning it runs by night and day with no pause and no settling, until Allah folds it up on the Day of Resurrection.

Whoever opposed the *mushaf* (the written codex of the Qur'an) argued: "I read according to the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas." Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: This is false and rejected against the one who transmitted it, because Abu 'Amr narrated from Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas; and Ibn Kathir narrated from Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿And the sun runs on to a resting place for it.﴾ These two chains from Ibn Abbas, whose soundness is witnessed by the *ijma'* (consensus of scholars), nullify what was narrated through a weak chain that contradicts the position of the majority and what the Muslim community has agreed upon.

I say: The established hadiths that we have mentioned refute his saying. How bold he is against the Book of Allah; may Allah fight him.

His saying: "li-mustaqarrin lahā" (لمستقر لها) means "to its resting place," and *al-mustaqarr* (المستقر) is the place of rest.

﴿That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.﴾ That is, that which has been mentioned of the matter of the night and the day, and the sun, is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.

**Verse 37–38**

Allah's saying: ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip away from it the day, and behold, they are in darkness.﴾ That is, a sign and an indication of Allah's oneness, His power, and the necessity of His divinity.

*Al-salkh* (السلخ) means to strip off and pull out. It is said: "Allah stripped him of his religion" (سلخه الله من دينه). It is then used in the sense of extracting. The disappearance of light and the coming of darkness have been treated as being like the stripping of something and the appearance of what was stripped, so this is a metaphor (*isti'arah*). *Muzlimun* (مظلمون) means "those who have entered into darkness." It is said: "adhlamna" (أظلمنا), meaning we entered the darkness of the night; "adhharna" (أظهرنا), meaning we entered the time of midday (*zuhr*). Likewise "asbahna" (أصبحنا), "adhha naa" (أضحينا), and "amsayna" (أمسينا). It has been said that *minhu* (منه) means *ankhu* (عنه), and the meaning is: We strip away from it the light of the day. "Fa-idha hum muzlimun" means: they are in darkness, because the light of the day spreads through the air and illuminates it; when it departs from it, the air becomes dark.

Allah's saying: ﴿And the sun runs on to a resting place for it.﴾ It is permissible for its estimated construction to be: "And a sign for them is the sun." It is also permissible for *al-shams* (الشمس) to be in the nominative by the implied presence of a verb that the following word explains. It is also permissible for it to be nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), with *tajri* (تجري) in the position of the predicate, meaning "running."
