Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 39:

There are three issues in this.

The first: His saying, Exalted is He, "وَالْقَمَرَ" (and the moon). Its implied construction is: "وَآيَةٌ لَهُمُ الْقَمَرُ" (and a sign for them is the moon). It is also permissible for "وَالْقَمَرُ" to be in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'). The Kufans read "وَالْقَمَرَ" in the accusative, by supposing an implied verb, and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd. He said: "Because before it there is a verb and after it there is a verb: before it "نَسْلَخُ" (We strip off) and after it "قَدَّرْناهُ" (We have measured it)." Al-Nahhas said: Men of Arabic grammar, as far as I know, all disagree with what he said, including al-Farra', who said: "The nominative is more pleasing to me." The nominative is preferred by them because it is coordinated (ma'tuf) on what precedes it, and its meaning is "وَآيَةٌ لَهُمُ الْقَمَرُ." As for his saying that before it is "نَسْلَخُ," the nearer item before it is "تَجْرِي" and before that "وَالشَّمْسُ" in the nominative. And what he mentioned after it, namely "قَدَّرْناهُ," has already governed the pronoun (the ha'). Abu Hatim said: "The nominative is preferable, because you have occupied the verb away from it with the pronoun, so you put it in the nominative by the inchoative (ibtida')." It is said: "The moon is not the mansions (manazil), so how does He say 'قَدَّرْناهُ مَنازِلَ' (We have measured it as mansions)?" There are two answers to this. One: "قَدَّرْناهُ" means "we have measured it, being mansions," like "وَسْئَلِ الْقَرْيَةَ" (Yusuf 82). The other measure: "قَدَّرْنا لَهُ مَنَازِلَ" (We measured for it mansions), then the lam was deleted, and its deletion is good because the verb transitively takes two objects, like "وَاخْتارَ مُوسى قَوْمَهُ سَبْعِينَ رَجُلًا" (A'raf 155). The mansions are twenty-eight mansions; the moon descends into one of them each night. They are: al-Sharatan, al-Butayn, al-Thurayya, al-Dabaran, al-Haq'a, al-Han'a, al-Dhira', al-Nathra, al-Tarf, al-Jabha, al-Kharatan, al-Sarfa, al-Awwa', al-Simak, al-Ghafr, al-Zubanayan, al-Iklil, al-Qalb, al-Shawla, al-Na'a'im, al-Balda, Sa'd al-Dhabih, Sa'd Bula', Sa'd al-Su'ud, Sa'd al-Akhbiya, al-Far' al-Muqaddam, al-Far' al-Mu'akhkhar, Batn al-Hut. When the moon reaches the last of them, it returns to the first, and it traverses the orbit in twenty-eight nights. Then it hides, then rises as a crescent, and it returns in traversing the orbit through the mansions. These are divided among the zodiac signs, with each sign having two and a third mansions. So for Aries (al-Hamal) there are al-Sharatan, al-Butayn and a third of al-Thurayya; for Taurus (al-Thawr) there are two thirds of al-Thurayya, al-Dabaran and two thirds of al-Haq'a; and so on through the rest. The naming of the zodiac signs has already passed in "al-Hijr" (see vol. 10, p. 9, first or second edition). And Allah is to be praised. 

It is said: Allah Exalted created the sun and the moon from fire, then they were clothed with light at their rising. The light of the sun is from the light of the Throne, and the light of the moon is from the light of the Footstool (Kursi). That is the origin of the creation and this is the covering. As for the sun, its covering was left in its state so that it would blaze and shine. As for the moon, the Trusted Spirit (Jibril) placed a wing upon its face, and it erased its light by the power of the wing, for he is a spirit, and the spirit's authority prevails over things. That erasure remained as the creatures see it. Then it was placed in a sheath of water, and then a course was made for it, so every night there appears to the creatures from that sheath a moon in the measure that it is illuminated for them, until its emergence is complete and they see it in its totality and roundness. Then every night some of it returns to the sheath, so it diminishes in sight and in illumination by the measure that it increased at the beginning. It begins to wane from the side that the sun does not see, which is the side of setting, until it returns like the old 'urjun, which is the dried, curved cluster stalk of the palm, thin and withered. The moon is so called because it "yuqmir," that is, it whitens the air with its whiteness until it hides.

The second: "حَتَّى عادَ كَالْعُرْجُونِ الْقَدِيمِ" (until it returned like the old 'urjun). Al-Zajjaj said: It is the stalk of the cluster on which the strands are, and it is on the pattern of fu'lun from al-in'iraj, which is bending; that is, it travelled through its mansions, and when it is at the end of them it becomes thin, curved and narrow until it becomes like the 'urjun. On this view the nun is extra (za'ida). Qatada said: It is the dry, bent cluster of the palm tree. Tha'lab said regarding "كَالْعُرْجُونِ الْقَدِيمِ": "كَالْعُرْجُونِ" is what remains of the kibasa on the palm when it is cut, and "الْقَدِيمِ" is the worn-out. Al-Khalil, in the section on quadriliteral roots, said: "al-'Urjun" is the base of the cluster, yellowish and broad, to which the crescent is likened when it bends. Al-Jawhari said: "al-'Urjun" is the base of the cluster that curves, from which the strands are cut, so it remains on the palm dry; and 'arjanahu means he struck him with the 'urjun. According to these, the nun is original. From this is the verse of A'sha Bani Qays:

Fragrant with musk and ambergris therein... and yellow like the 'urjun of the moon.

When the 'urjun ages, dries and bends, the moon is likened to it in its thinness and yellowness. It is also called al-Ihan, al-Kibasa and al-Qinw, and the people of Egypt call it al-Isbatula. It is read "الْعِرْجَوْنِ" on the pattern of "الْفِرْجَوْنِ," and both are dialect forms, like al-Buzyun and al-Bizyawn. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned this and said: It is the stalk of the cluster between its strands down to its root on the palm.

Know that the year is divided into four seasons, each season having seven mansions. The first is spring (al-Rabi'), beginning fifteen days into Adhar, and its days number ninety-two, during which the sun traverses three signs: Aries, Taurus and Gemini (al-Jawza'), and seven mansions: al-Sharatan, al-Butayn, al-Thurayya, al-Dabaran, al-Haq'a, al-Han'a and al-Dhira'. Then summer begins fifteen days into Huzayran, and its days number ninety-two, during which the sun traverses three signs: Cancer (al-Sharatan), Leo (al-Asad) and Virgo (al-Sunbula), and seven mansions: al-Nathra, al-Tarf, al-Jabha, al-Kharatan, al-Sarfa, al-Awwa' and al-Simak. Then autumn begins fifteen days into Aylul, and its days number ninety-one, during which the sun traverses three signs: Libra (al-Mizan), Scorpio (al-'Aqrab) and Sagittarius (al-Qaws), and seven mansions: al-Ghafr, al-Zubanan, al-Iklil, al-Qalb, al-Shawla, al-Na'a'im and al-Balda. Then winter begins fifteen days into Kanun al-Awwal, and its days number ninety, and perhaps ninety-one, during which the sun traverses three signs: Capricorn (al-Jadi), Aquarius (al-Dalw) and Pisces (al-Hut), and seven mansions: Sa'd al-Dhabih, Sa'd Bula', Sa'd al-Su'ud, Sa'd al-Akhbiya, al-Far' al-Muqaddam, al-Far' al-Mu'akhkhar and Batn al-Hut. This is the division of the Syriac (al-Suryaniyyun) for their months: Tishrin al-Awwal, Tishrin al-Thani, Kanun al-Awwal, Kanun al-Thani, Ashbat, Adhar, Nisan, Ayyar, Huzayran, Tammuz, Ab, Aylul. All of them have thirty-one days except Tishrin al-Thani, Nisan, Huzayran and Aylul, which have thirty days, and Ashbat has twenty-eight days and a quarter of a day.

We only intended by this that you should consider the power of Allah Exalted, and that is His saying: "وَالْقَمَرَ قَدَّرْناهُ مَنازِلَ" (We have measured for the moon mansions). When the sun is in a mansion, the crescent appears with the mansion after it, and dawn is two mansions before it. When the sun is at al-Thurayya on the twenty-fifth or so of Nisan, dawn is at al-Sharatan, and the crescent appears at al-Dabaran. Then it has one mansion each night until it traverses in twenty-eight nights twenty-eight mansions. The sun has traversed two mansions, so it traverses them, then it rises in the mansion after the sun's mansion. "ذلِكَ تَقْدِيرُ الْعَزِيزِ الْعَلِيمِ" (That is the measuring of the Mighty, the All-Knowing).

The third: His saying, "الْقَدِيمِ" (the old). Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-Qadim" is the one that has passed a year, and when it becomes old it becomes thin, bent and yellow, so the moon is likened to it in three respects. It is said: the least period for something described as "qadim" is one year. So if a man says: "Every slave of mine that is qadim is free," or writes this in his will, then whoever has been with him for a year or more is freed. I say: What follows from the crescents of legal rulings has already passed in "al-Baqara" (see vol. 2, pp. 341 ff., second edition), and Allah is to be praised.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 40:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon﴾. The word *al-shams* (the sun) is in the nominative case (*rufi'at*) as the subject of a nominal sentence (*al-ibtida'*, the inchoative). *La* (not) cannot govern a definite noun (*ma'rifah*), so it does not govern *al-shams*. The scholars have discussed the meaning of this verse. Some of them said: its meaning is that the sun does not overtake the moon and thereby nullify its (the moon's) function. That is, each of the two has its own authority (*sultan*) in its own sphere, so neither enters upon the other and takes away its authority, until God nullifies what He has ordained concerning that, and the sun rises from its west, as explained earlier at the end of surah *al-An'am* [[See vol. 7, p. 145 and what follows, first or second edition.]].

It was also said: when the sun rises, there is no light for the moon, and when the moon rises, there is no light for the sun. This meaning was related from Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak. Mujahid said: that is, the light of one of them does not resemble the light of the other. Qatada said: each has a limit and a knowledge that it does not exceed, nor fall short of; when the authority of this one comes, the authority of that one departs. Al-Hasan said: the two do not meet in the sky specifically on the night of the new moon, meaning the sun does not remain until the moon rises; rather, when the sun sets, the moon rises. Yahya ibn Sallam said: the sun does not overtake the moon specifically on the night of the full moon, because the moon hastens to set before the sun rises.

It was also said: the meaning is that if the two are together in the sky, one of them is in front of the other in stations (*manazil*) in which they do not share. This was also said by Ibn Abbas. It was said: the moon is in the lowest heaven and the sun is in the fourth heaven, so it does not overtake it; this was mentioned by al-Nahhas and al-Mahdawi. Al-Nahhas said: the best and clearest of what has been said about its meaning, and the one least open to objection, is that the course of the moon is swift, and the sun cannot overtake it in its course; this was also mentioned by al-Mahdawi.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the sun and the moon are brought together﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 9], that is when He holds back the sun from rising, as explained earlier at the end of surah *al-An'am* [[See vol. 7, p. 146, second edition.]], and it will come again in surah *al-Qiyamah* as well. Their being brought together is a sign of the end of this world and the establishment of the Hour.

"And each" means of the sun, the moon and the stars "in an orbit they swim" (*yasbahun*), that is, they move along. It was also said: they revolve. He did not say *tasbahu* (feminine singular), because He described them with the action of those who reason (*man ya'qilu*). Al-Hasan said: the sun, the moon and the stars are in an orbit between the heaven and the earth, not attached to them; if they were attached, they would not move. This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi and al-Mawardi.

Some scholars cited His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nor does the night outstrip the day﴾ as evidence that the day was created before the night, and that the night did not precede it in creation. It was said: each of them comes at its appointed time and does not precede its companion, until the sun and the moon are joined together on the Day of Resurrection, as He said: ﴿And the sun and the moon are brought together﴾. The present alternation is only so that the interests of the servants may be fulfilled, ﴿that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ [Yunus: 5], and so that the night may be for rest and repose, and the day for activity, as He said, may He be exalted: ﴿And of His mercy He made for you night and day, that you may rest therein and seek of His bounty﴾ [al-Qasas: 73]. And He said: ﴿And We made your sleep a rest﴾ [al-Naba': 9], that is, a repose for your bodies from the labour of the day.

So His saying ﴿nor does the night outstrip the day﴾ means: the night does not overcome the day. It is said: *sabaqa fulan fulanan*, meaning he overcame him. Al-Mubarrad mentioned that he said: I heard Umara reciting ﴿wa-la al-layl sabiq al-nahar﴾ (with *sabiq* in the nominative and *al-nahar* in the accusative). I said: what is this? He said: I meant *sabiqun al-nahar*, but I dropped the tanwin (nunation) because it is lighter. Al-Nahhas said: it is possible that *al-nahar* is in the accusative without tanwin, and that the tanwin was dropped because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 41–44:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And a sign for them﴾ may have three meanings. The first: a lesson for them, because there is consideration (i'tibar) in the signs. The second: a blessing upon them, because there is favour in the signs. The third: a warning for them, because there is admonition in the signs. ﴿That We carried their offspring﴾ [[ "Dhurriyyatahum" in the plural is the reading of Nafi'.]] ﴿in the laden ship﴾ is among the most difficult (ashkal) things in the surah, because they themselves are the ones being carried. It is said the meaning is: "And a sign for the people of Makkah: that We carried the offspring of the past generations" ﴿in the laden ship﴾. Thus the two pronouns differ; this was mentioned by al-Mahdawi. Al-Nahhas related it from Ali ibn Sulayman, that he heard him say it. It is also said: both pronouns refer to the people of Makkah, on the basis that their offspring (dhurriyyat) are their children and their weak ones. Then "the ship" in the first view is the ship of Nuh. In the second view it is a generic noun (ism li-l-jins): He, Mighty and Majestic, informed with His kindness and favour that He created ships in which He carries those who are carried in them, from among those who find walking and riding difficult, from among the protected (dhimmah) and the weak. On this view the two pronouns agree. It is also said: the dhurriyyah are the fathers and forefathers, whom Allah carried in the ship of Nuh, peace be upon him. Thus the fathers are offspring and the sons are offspring, by the evidence of this verse; this was said by Abu Uthman. The fathers were called dhurriyyah because from them the sons were produced (dhara'a). A fourth view: the dhurriyyah are the sperm-drops (nutaf) which Allah carried in the wombs of women, likened to the laden ship; this was said by Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and mentioned by al-Mawardi. The derivation of dhurriyyah has already passed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 107 and following, second edition.]], and the discussion of it is complete there. And "al-mashhun" means the filled, loaded. And "al-fulk" may be singular or plural. Its discussion has already preceded in Yunus [[See vol. 8, p. 324, second edition.]].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We created for them of its likeness that they ride﴾. The original is "yarkabunahu," and the hā' was dropped due to the length of the phrase [[Thus in all copies of the original text; in I'rab al-Quran of al-Nahhas:]] and because it is the end of a verse (ra's ayah). Regarding its meaning there are three opinions. The view of Mujahid, Qatadah, and a group of the exegetes; and it is related from Ibn Abbas that the meaning of "of its likeness" is the camels: He created them for them to ride on land, like the ships ridden on the sea, and the Arabs compare camels to ships. Tarafah said:

As if the litters (hudūj) of the Malikiyyah at dawn,
and the large ships (khalāyā safīn) among the wide plains (nawāsif) of Dadd.
[[The hudaj is a type of women's riding litter. The Malikiyyah are attributed to Malik ibn Sa'd ibn Dubay'ah. The tawasif are plural of nasifah, a wide open courtyard found in a valley. Dadd is a place.]]

Khalāyā is the plural of khaliyyah, which is the great ship. The second view is that it refers to camels, beasts and everything that is ridden. The third view is that it refers to ships. Al-Nahhas said: this is the most sound of them, because its chain of transmission from Ibn Abbas is connected. ﴿And We created for them of its likeness that they ride﴾: he said, He created for them ships like them in which they ride. Abu Malik said: they are the small ships, created like the large ships, and this is related from Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan. Al-Dahhak and others said: they are the ships made after the ship of Nuh. Al-Mawardi said: and it follows from the implication of the interpretation of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that the dhurriyyah in the laden ship are the sperm-drops in the wombs of women, that there is a fifth view on His saying: ﴿And We created for them of its likeness that they ride﴾, namely that its interpretation is that women were created for the riding of husbands; but I have not seen this related.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if We will, We drown them﴾, i.e., in the sea, so the pronoun returns either to the possessors of the offspring or to all of them. This indicates the correctness of the saying of Ibn Abbas and of whoever said that the intended meaning of "of its likeness" is ships, not camels. ﴿Then there is no one to cry out for them﴾, i.e., no helper for them; this was narrated by Sa'id from Qatadah. Shaybān related from him: "then there is no defence for them," and their meanings are close. "Sarikh" means "musrikh" (one who cries out for help), the form fa'il in the sense of fa'il. It is permissible to read "fa-la sarikhun lahum" (with raf'), because what follows it admits only the nominative, being definite, namely ﴿nor are they rescued﴾. The grammarians prefer "la rajul fi al-dar wa la Zayd." The meaning of "yunqadhun" is "they are delivered from drowning"; and it is said: from punishment. ﴿Except as a mercy from Us﴾. Al-Kisa'i said: it is in the accusative as an exception. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the accusative of the object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), i.e., for mercy. ﴿And enjoyment﴾ is conjoined to it. ﴿For a time﴾: until death, said Qatadah. Yahya ibn Sallam said: until the Resurrection. That is, except that We have mercy on them and let them enjoy until their appointed terms; and Allah hastened the punishment of the earlier nations and deferred the punishment of the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ), even if they denied him, until death and the Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 45–50:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Beware of what is before you and what is behind you,"﴾ Qatadah said: He means, "Beware of what is before you," i.e., of the events concerning the nations who came before you, "and what is behind you," i.e., of the Hereafter. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid said: "What is before you" is the sins that have passed, "and what is behind you" is the sins that will come. Al-Hasan said: "What is before you" is what has passed of your term (ajal), "and what is behind you" is what remains of it. It was also said: "What is before you" is of this world, "and what is behind you" is of the punishment of the Hereafter, said Sufyan. Al-Tha'labi related the reverse of this view from Ibn 'Abbas. He said: "What is before you" is of the matter of the Hereafter and what you have done for it, "and what is behind you" is of the matter of this world, so beware of it and do not be deceived by it. It was also said: "What is before you" is what is apparent to you, "and what is behind you" is what is hidden from you. The answer (jawab) is omitted, and the implied meaning is: when it is said to them thus, they turn away. The evidence for this is His saying after it: ﴿And no sign of the signs of their Lord comes to them but that they turn away from it﴾, so this suffices in place of that.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what Allah has provided you,"﴾ i.e., give charity to the poor. Al-Hasan said: He means the Jews, who were commanded to feed the poor. It was also said: they are the polytheists, who said to the poor Companions of the Prophet ﷺ: "Give us from your wealth that you claim belongs to Allah." This is His saying: ﴿And they assign to Allah a portion of what He has produced of tillage and cattle﴾ [al-An'am: 136]. So they deprived them and said: "If Allah willed, He would feed you," mockingly, "so we will not feed you until you return to our religion." They said, "Shall we feed one whom, if Allah willed, He would have fed?" i.e., shall we provide sustenance to one whom, if Allah willed, He would have fed? That had reached them from the words of the Muslims, that the Provider is Allah. So they said in mockery: "Shall we provide for one whom, if Allah willed, He would have enriched?" It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: there were heretics (zanadiqah) in Mecca, and when they were commanded to give charity to the needy, they said: "No, by Allah! Shall Allah make him poor and we feed him?" They used to hear the believers attach the actions of Allah, exalted is He, to His will, saying: "If Allah willed, He would have enriched so-and-so, and if Allah willed, He would have made him mighty, and if Allah willed, it would have been thus." ﴿"So they will not be able to make a bequest"﴾, i.e., none of them will be able to bequeath anything to another for what is in his hand of right. It was also said: they will not be able to advise one another to repent and to desist, but will die in their markets and places. ﴿"Nor to their families will they return."﴾ When they die. It was also said: the meaning of "nor to their families will they return" is that they will not return to them with words. Qatadah said: "nor to their families will they return," i.e., to their dwellings, because they were hurried away from that.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 51–54:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Horn is blown﴾. This is the second blast, for resurrection (al-nash'ah). We have already explained in Surah "al-Naml" [[See vol. 13, p. 239, first or second edition.]] that there are two blasts, not three, and this verse points to that. Al-Mubarak ibn Fadalah narrated from al-Hasan, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Between the two blasts is forty years. The first, by which Allah causes every living thing to die, and the second, by which Allah brings back to life every dead thing." Qatadah said: "al-Sur" is the plural of "suratun" (form), meaning that the souls are blown into the forms. "Sura" and "sur" are like "surah," as al-Ajjaj said:

How many a one in a curtained enclosure, I traveled to him over the high walls.

It has been narrated from Abu Hurairah that he recited "wa-nufikha fi al-sur." Al-Nahhas said: The correct reading is "al-Sur" with a sukun on the waw, meaning the horn. This is transmitted by authoritative report from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it is well known in Arabic speech. The lexicographers recited:

We struck them on the morning of al-Ghawrayn, with galloping horses in the dust of the two clouds of dust,

a fierce striking, not like the striking of the two horns.

This has already been discussed fully in "al-An'am" [[See vol. 7, p. 20 onward, first or second edition.]]. "Then they, from the graves (al-ajdath)," that is, from the tombs. It is also read with a fa', "min al-ajdaf," mentioned by al-Zamakhshari. It is said: jadath and jadaf. The eloquent form is jadath with a tha', and its plural is ajdath and ajdath. Al-Mutanakhkhil al-Hudhali said:

I recognized by ajdath and Naʿaf Irq, marks like the decoration of carpets.

And ijtadatha means he took for himself a tomb. "To their Lord they will hasten (yansilun)," that is, they will come out, as said by Ibn Abbas and Qatadah. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qais:

So take off your garments from your garments, and come out.

From it also comes the word nasl for offspring, because it comes out from its mother's belly. It is also said: they will hurry. Al-nasalan and al-'asalan mean quick movement in walking, and from it is the gait of the wolf. The poet said:

The gait of the wolf, when it became near and the night grew cold upon it, and it hastened.

It is said: 'asala al-dhi'b wa-nasala, ya'silu and yansilu, from the pattern of daraba yadribu. It is also said yansulu with a damma. It means to hurry in walking, so the meaning is: they will come out hastening. In the Revelation: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are only as a single soul﴾ [Luqman: 28], and He said: ﴿They will come out of the graves as if they were scattered locusts﴾ [al-Qamar: 7], and in "Sa'ala sa'il": ﴿On the day they come out of the graves swiftly, as if they were rushing to a goal﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 43], meaning they hasten. In a report: We complained to the Prophet (ﷺ) about weakness, and he said: "Upon you is al-nasl," meaning hastening in walking, for it energizes.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will say: O woe to us!﴾ Ibn al-Anbari said: "ya wailana" is a good pause, then one begins "man ba'athana." It is narrated from some readers: "ya wailana min ba'thina," with kasra on min and the tha' of al-ba'th. This is narrated from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him). According to this view, it is not good to pause at "ya wailana" until one says "min marqadina." In the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "man habbana" joined "min marqadina." This is evidence for the soundness of the view of the common reading. Al-Mahdawi said: Ibn Abi Layla read: "qalu ya wailatana," with the addition of a ta' which is the feminine of connection, and similar is: ﴿O woe to me! Shall I bear a child while I am an old woman?﴾ [Hud: 72]. Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) read "ya wailata min ba'thina," so "min" is connected to the woe, or is a circumstantial clause from "wailata," and it is connected to a deleted element, as if he said: O woe, being from our resurrection. Just as it may be a predicate for it, so it may be a circumstantial clause from it. The "min" in "min marqadina" is connected to the resurrection itself.

Then it is asked: how could they say this when they are among those punished in their graves? The answer is that Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: they sleep a sleep. In another narration: they say, "O woe to us, who woke us from our sleeping place?" Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: this report should not be taken to mean that "ahhabana" is part of the words of the Qur'an, as one who slandered the Qur'an claimed, but it is an explanation of "ba'athana" or expresses some of its meanings. Abu Bakr said: I also memorized it as "man habbana" without an alif in ahhabana, with the nun of man pronounced with sukun. The correct form in terms of language is "man ahhabana" with a fatha on the nun, as the fatha of the hamza of ahabba was transferred to the nun of "man" and the hamza was dropped, as the Arabs say: "man akhbaraka? man a'lamaka?" meaning "man akhbaraka?" It is said: ahbabtu al-na'im, fa-habba al-na'im (I woke the sleeper, and the sleeper woke). Ahmad ibn Yahya the grammarian recited to us:

And a blaming woman who woke me in the night and rebuked me, and no reproacher had reproached me before that.

Abu Salih said: When the first blast is blown, the punishment is lifted from the people of the graves, and they doze a doze until the second blast, and between them is forty years. That is their saying: "Who woke us from our resting place?" Ibn Abbas and Qatadah said likewise. The scholars of meanings said: When the disbelievers see Hell and the various kinds of punishment in it, what they were punished with in their graves becomes like sleep beside its punishment. Mujahid said: The believers then said to them: "This is what the Most Merciful promised." Qatadah said: Those whom Allah guided said to them: "This is what the Most Merciful promised." Al-Farra' said: The angels said to them: "This is what the Most Merciful promised." Al-Nahhas said: These opinions agree, because the angels are among the believers and among those whom Allah guided, azza wa-jall. On this basis is interpreted the saying of Allah, azza wa-jall: ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds, they are the best of creation﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 7], and likewise the hadith: "The believer is better in the sight of Allah than everything He created." It is possible that the angels and others among the believers said to them: "This is what the Most Merciful promised." It is also said: When some of the disbelievers said to one another: "Who raised us from our resting place?" they confirmed the messengers when they saw what the messengers had told them about, then they said: "This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth," but they had denied it, so they acknowledged it when acknowledgment no longer benefited them. Hafs used to pause at "min marqadina" and then begin, saying: "hadha." Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari said: "man ba'athana min marqadina" is a good pause, then one begins: "hadha ma wa'ada al-Rahman." It is also permissible to pause at "marqadina hadha," making "hadha" in the genitive by following "marqad," and to begin: "ma wa'ada al-Rahman," in the sense: your resurrection is what the Most Merciful promised, that is, the promise of the Most Merciful raised you. Al-Nahhas said: The complete pause is at "min marqadina," and "hadha" is in the nominative position as the subject, with its predicate being "ma wa'ada al-Rahman." It is also permissible that it is in the genitive position as an adjective of "marqadina," so the complete pause is "min marqadina hadha." "Ma wa'ada al-Rahman" is in the nominative position from three aspects. Abu Ishaq mentioned two of them, saying: it is by the implication of "hadha." The second aspect is that it means: "Truly, what the Most Merciful promised of your resurrection." The third aspect is that it means: "What the Most Merciful promised."

﴿It was but one shout﴾, meaning their resurrection and revival were by a single shout, which is the saying of Israfil: "O decayed bones, scattered joints and torn hair! Indeed Allah commands you to gather for the judgment." This is the meaning of the saying of the Truth: ﴿On the day they hear the Cry in truth, that is the Day of Coming Out﴾ [Qaf: 42]. And He said: ﴿Hastening toward the Caller﴾ [al-Qamar: 8], as will come. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, if it is authentically transmitted from him: "in kanat illa zaqyatan wahidatan," and al-zaqyah is the shout, which has already been mentioned.

﴿Then they, all of them, will be brought before Us﴾: "fa-idha hum" is the subject, and "jami'un," being indefinite, is the predicate, and "muhdarun" is its adjective. The meaning of "muhdarun" is "gathered," brought to the place of reckoning, like His saying: ﴿And the matter of the Hour is but as a glance of the eye﴾ [al-Nahl: 77].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So today no soul will be wronged in anything﴾, that is, nothing will be reduced from the reward of its deed. ﴿And you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾. "Mimma" is in the accusative position in two respects. The first is that it is a second object of the passive verb. The second is by removing the preposition of the attribute; its estimate is: "illa bi-ma kuntum ta'malun," meaning "ta'malunahu," so it was deleted.

It is also permissible to pause at "marqadina hadha," making "hadha" in the genitive by following "marqad," and to begin: "ma wa'ada al-Rahman," in the sense: your resurrection is what the Most Merciful promised, that is, the promise of the Most Merciful raised you. Al-Nahhas said: The complete pause is at "min marqadina," and "hadha" is in the nominative position as the subject, with its predicate being "ma wa'ada al-Rahman." It is also permissible that it is in the genitive position as an adjective of "marqadina," so the complete pause is "min marqadina hadha." "Ma wa'ada al-Rahman" is in the nominative position from three aspects. Abu Ishaq mentioned two of them, saying: it is by the implication of "hadha." The second aspect is that it means: "Truly, what the Most Merciful promised of your resurrection." The third aspect is that it means: "What the Most Merciful promised."

﴿It was but one shout﴾, meaning their resurrection and revival were by a single shout, which is the saying of Israfil: "O decayed bones, scattered joints and torn hair! Indeed Allah commands you to gather for the judgment." This is the meaning of the saying of the Truth: ﴿On the day they hear the Cry in truth, that is the Day of Coming Out﴾ [Qaf: 42]. And He said: ﴿Hastening toward the Caller﴾ [al-Qamar: 8], as will come. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, if it is authentically transmitted from him: "in kanat illa zaqyatan wahidatan," and al-zaqyah is the shout, which has already been mentioned.

﴿Then they, all of them, will be brought before Us﴾: "fa-idha hum" is the subject, and "jami'un," being indefinite, is the predicate, and "muhdarun" is its adjective. The meaning of "muhdarun" is "gathered," brought to the place of reckoning, like His saying: ﴿And the matter of the Hour is but as a glance of the eye﴾ [al-Nahl: 77].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So today no soul will be wronged in anything﴾, that is, nothing will be reduced from the reward of its deed. ﴿And you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾. "Mimma" is in the accusative position in two respects. The first is that it is a second object of the passive verb. The second is by removing the preposition of the attribute; its estimate is: "illa bi-ma kuntum ta'malun," meaning "ta'malunahu," so it was deleted.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 51–54:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Horn is blown﴾. This is the second blast, for resurrection (al-nash'ah). We have already explained in Surah "al-Naml" [[See vol. 13, p. 239, first or second edition.]] that there are two blasts, not three, and this verse points to that. Al-Mubarak ibn Fadalah narrated from al-Hasan, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Between the two blasts is forty years. The first, by which Allah causes every living thing to die, and the second, by which Allah brings back to life every dead thing." Qatadah said: "al-Sur" is the plural of "suratun" (form), meaning that the souls are blown into the forms. "Sura" and "sur" are like "surah," as al-Ajjaj said:

How many a one in a curtained enclosure, I traveled to him over the high walls.

It has been narrated from Abu Hurairah that he recited "wa-nufikha fi al-sur." Al-Nahhas said: The correct reading is "al-Sur" with a sukun on the waw, meaning the horn. This is transmitted by authoritative report from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it is well known in Arabic speech. The lexicographers recited:

We struck them on the morning of al-Ghawrayn, with galloping horses in the dust of the two clouds of dust,

a fierce striking, not like the striking of the two horns.

This has already been discussed fully in "al-An'am" [[See vol. 7, p. 20 onward, first or second edition.]]. "Then they, from the graves (al-ajdath)," that is, from the tombs. It is also read with a fa', "min al-ajdaf," mentioned by al-Zamakhshari. It is said: jadath and jadaf. The eloquent form is jadath with a tha', and its plural is ajdath and ajdath. Al-Mutanakhkhil al-Hudhali said:

I recognized by ajdath and Naʿaf Irq, marks like the decoration of carpets.

And ijtadatha means he took for himself a tomb. "To their Lord they will hasten (yansilun)," that is, they will come out, as said by Ibn Abbas and Qatadah. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qais:

So take off your garments from your garments, and come out.

From it also comes the word nasl for offspring, because it comes out from its mother's belly. It is also said: they will hurry. Al-nasalan and al-'asalan mean quick movement in walking, and from it is the gait of the wolf. The poet said:

The gait of the wolf, when it became near and the night grew cold upon it, and it hastened.

It is said: 'asala al-dhi'b wa-nasala, ya'silu and yansilu, from the pattern of daraba yadribu. It is also said yansulu with a damma. It means to hurry in walking, so the meaning is: they will come out hastening. In the Revelation: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are only as a single soul﴾ [Luqman: 28], and He said: ﴿They will come out of the graves as if they were scattered locusts﴾ [al-Qamar: 7], and in "Sa'ala sa'il": ﴿On the day they come out of the graves swiftly, as if they were rushing to a goal﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 43], meaning they hasten. In a report: We complained to the Prophet (ﷺ) about weakness, and he said: "Upon you is al-nasl," meaning hastening in walking, for it energizes.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will say: O woe to us!﴾ Ibn al-Anbari said: "ya wailana" is a good pause, then one begins "man ba'athana." It is narrated from some readers: "ya wailana min ba'thina," with kasra on min and the tha' of al-ba'th. This is narrated from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him). According to this view, it is not good to pause at "ya wailana" until one says "min marqadina." In the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "man habbana" joined "min marqadina." This is evidence for the soundness of the view of the common reading. Al-Mahdawi said: Ibn Abi Layla read: "qalu ya wailatana," with the addition of a ta' which is the feminine of connection, and similar is: ﴿O woe to me! Shall I bear a child while I am an old woman?﴾ [Hud: 72]. Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) read "ya wailata min ba'thina," so "min" is connected to the woe, or is a circumstantial clause from "wailata," and it is connected to a deleted element, as if he said: O woe, being from our resurrection. Just as it may be a predicate for it, so it may be a circumstantial clause from it. The "min" in "min marqadina" is connected to the resurrection itself.

Then it is asked: how could they say this when they are among those punished in their graves? The answer is that Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: they sleep a sleep. In another narration: they say, "O woe to us, who woke us from our sleeping place?" Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: this report should not be taken to mean that "ahhabana" is part of the words of the Qur'an, as one who slandered the Qur'an claimed, but it is an explanation of "ba'athana" or expresses some of its meanings. Abu Bakr said: I also memorized it as "man habbana" without an alif in ahhabana, with the nun of man pronounced with sukun. The correct form in terms of language is "man ahhabana" with a fatha on the nun, as the fatha of the hamza of ahabba was transferred to the nun of "man" and the hamza was dropped, as the Arabs say: "man akhbaraka? man a'lamaka?" meaning "man akhbaraka?" It is said: ahbabtu al-na'im, fa-habba al-na'im (I woke the sleeper, and the sleeper woke). Ahmad ibn Yahya the grammarian recited to us:

And a blaming woman who woke me in the night and rebuked me, and no reproacher had reproached me before that.

Abu Salih said: When the first blast is blown, the punishment is lifted from the people of the graves, and they doze a doze until the second blast, and between them is forty years. That is their saying: "Who woke us from our resting place?" Ibn Abbas and Qatadah said likewise. The scholars of meanings said: When the disbelievers see Hell and the various kinds of punishment in it, what they were punished with in their graves becomes like sleep beside its punishment. Mujahid said: The believers then said to them: "This is what the Most Merciful promised." Qatadah said: Those whom Allah guided said to them: "This is what the Most Merciful promised." Al-Farra' said: The angels said to them: "This is what the Most Merciful promised." Al-Nahhas said: These opinions agree, because the angels are among the believers and among those whom Allah guided, azza wa-jall. On this basis is interpreted the saying of Allah, azza wa-jall: ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds, they are the best of creation﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 7], and likewise the hadith: "The believer is better in the sight of Allah than everything He created." **Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 36, verses 55–59:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in joy, reclining.﴾ Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and Mujahid said: "Their occupation is deflowering the virgins" (*iftida' al-'adhara*).

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim mentioned in his book *Mushkil al-Quran*: Muhammad ibn Humayd al-Razi narrated to us, Ya'qub al-Qummi narrated to us, from Hafs ibn Humayd, from Shimr ibn 'Atiyyah, from Shaqiq ibn Salamah, from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, regarding His saying, "Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in joy," that he said: "Their occupation is deflowering the virgins."

Muhammad ibn Humayd narrated to us, Harun ibn al-Mughirah narrated to us, from Nahshal, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, similarly.

Abu Qilabah said: "While a man of the people of the Garden is with his wife, it is said to him, 'Turn to your wife,' and he says, 'I am occupied with my wife.' Then it is said, 'Turn also to your wife.'"

It was also said: "The companions of the Garden are busy with what they have of pleasures and delights, diverted from concern for the people of disobedience and their destination to the Fire, and from what they suffer of painful punishment, even if their relatives and family were among them." This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and others. Waki' said: "That is, in listening (to music)." Ibn Kaysan said: "'Busy' means visiting one another." It was also said: "They are in the hospitality of Allah, Exalted is He."

It is related that when the Day of Resurrection comes, a caller calls out: "Where are My servants who obeyed Me and guarded My covenant in the unseen?" They rise up, their faces like the full moon and the shining stars, riding on mounts of light whose reins are of ruby, flying with them over the heads of creation until they stand before the Throne. Then Allah, Majestic and Mighty, says to them: "Peace be upon My servants who obeyed Me and guarded My covenant in the unseen. I have chosen you, I have selected you, and I have preferred you. Go and enter the Garden without reckoning," and ﴿there is no fear upon you today, nor will you grieve﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 68]. (They pass over the Sirat like a flashing lightning, and its gates are opened for them.) Then the creation will be held in place at the gathering, and some will say to others: "O people, where is so-and-so and so-and-so?" At that time, some will be asking others, and a caller will call out: "Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in joy, reclining."

*Shughulin* and *shughlun* are two readings recited with both forms, like *ar-ru'ub* and *ar-ru'b*, and *as-suht* and *as-suht*, and this has been discussed before. [[See vol. 6, p. 184 of the printed edition.]]

*Fakihun*: al-Hasan said: "Joyful." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Happy." Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: "Admiring." Al-Suddi said: "Enjoying ease." The meanings are close. *Al-fukahah* is jesting and good speech. Abu Ja'far, Shaybah and al-A'raj read *fakihun* without an alif, and both are two dialects, like *al-farih* and *al-farih*, and *al-hadhir* and *al-hadhir*, as al-Farra' said. Al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubaydah said: *al-fakih* means one who possesses fruit, like *shahim* (fat-possessor), *lahim* (meat-possessor), *tamir* (date-possessor) and *labin* (milk-possessor), while *al-fakih* (in the sense of *al-mutafakkih*) means one who enjoys and one who lives in luxury. *Fakihun* without an alif, according to Qatadah, means "admiring." Abu Zayd said: "One says a man is *fakih* when he is good-natured and laughing."

Talhah ibn Musarrif read *fakihin* in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*).

﴿They and their spouses, in shades, upon couches, reclining﴾: *hum* is the subject and its predicate follows. It is permissible that *hum* be an emphatic pronoun, *wa-azwajuhum* be a conjunction upon the implied pronoun, and *muttaki'un* be an adjective of *fakihun*. The common reading is *fi zilalin* with a kasra on the *za'* and an alif. Ibn Mas'ud, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, al-A'mash, Yahya, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *fi zulalin* with a damma on the *za'* and without an alif. So *zilal* is the plural of *zill*, and *zulal* is the plural of *zullah*.

*'Ala al-arai'k*: this means the thrones in the canopied chambers. Its singular is *arikah*, like *safinah* and *safa'in*. The poet said:

"As if the redness of the rose upon its branches,
at the time of forenoon, in the garden of the one who laughs,
Are the cheeks of virgins who have blushed from shyness,
swaying with basil above the couches."

It is reported in a tradition from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whenever the people of the Garden have intercourse with their women, they return to being virgins." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Indeed, a man of the people of the Garden embraces the *hawra'* (a dark-eyed maiden) for seventy years, he does not tire of her and she does not tire of him. Whenever he comes to her, he finds her a virgin, and whenever he returns to her, his desire returns to him. He has intercourse with her with the strength of seventy men, and there is no emission between them. It comes without emission from him or from her."

﴿For them therein is fruit﴾: this is an inceptive clause with its predicate. ﴿And for them is whatever they call for﴾: the second *dal* in *yadda'una* is substituted from a *ta'*, because it is *yaftaʻilun* from *da'a*, meaning whoever asks for something is given it. This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah. So the meaning of *yadda'un* is "they wish," derived from *al-du'a'* (calling/asking). It was also said: the meaning is that whoever among them claims something, it is his, because Allah, Exalted is He, has disposed them so that none of them claims anything except what is fitting and good to claim. Yahya ibn Sallam said: *yadda'un* means "they desire." Ibn 'Abbas said: "They ask." The meanings are close.

Ibn al-Anbari said: "*Wa-lahum ma yadda'un*" is a good place to pause, and then you begin with *salam*, meaning: for them is peace. It is also permissible to make *salam* nominative, meaning: "and for them is whatever they call for, sealed/pure." On this view, it is not good to pause at *ma yadda'un*.

Al-Zajjaj said: *salam* is nominative as a substitute for *ma*, meaning: "and for them is that Allah sends peace upon them," and this is the wish of the people of the Garden. It is related from the hadith of Jarir ibn 'Abdullah al-Bajali that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "While the people of the Garden are in their bliss, a light shines upon them. They raise their heads, and behold, the Lord, Exalted is He, has looked down upon them from above, and He says: 'Peace be upon you, O people of the Garden.' That is His saying: '*Peace*, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful.' He looks at them, and they look at Him. They do not turn to anything of the bliss as long as they are looking at Him, until He veils Himself from them, and His light and blessings remain upon them in their homes." This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi and al-Qushayri. Its meaning is established in Sahih Muslim, and we have explained it in *Yunus* [[See vol. 8, p. 230 of the first printing]] at His saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best reward and more﴾ [Yunus: 26].

It is also permissible that *ma* be indefinite and *salam* an adjective of it, meaning: "and for them is whatever they call for, sealed." It is also permissible that *ma* be nominative by the inceptive, and *salam* the predicate of it. On these aspects, one does not pause at *wa-lahum ma yadda'un*.

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, *salaman* is a verbal noun (*masdar*), and if you wish, it can be in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning: "and for them is whatever they call for, with peace, or safety, or as something sealed." On this view, it is not good to pause at *yadda'un*.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi read *silm* as a new sentence, as if he said: "That is peace for them, they do not dispute about it." Then *wa-lahum ma yadda'un* is a complete sentence. It is also permissible that *salam* be a substitute for His saying *wa-lahum ma yadda'un*, and the predicate of *ma yadda'un* is *lahum*. It is also permissible that *salam* be another predicate, and the meaning of the statement is that it is theirs purely, without anyone disputing it.

*Qawlan* is a verbal noun, meaning: Allah says that, a saying; or He says it as a saying. The verb is omitted and its verbal noun indicates it. It is also permissible that the meaning be "and for them is whatever they call for, as a saying," that is, a promise from Allah. On this second view, it is not good to pause at *yadda'un*.

Al-Sijistani said: the pause at His saying *salam* is complete. This is an error, because *al-qawl* (the saying) is separate from what precedes it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And withdraw today, O criminals.﴾ It is said: *tamayyazu*, *amazu* and *amtazu* have the same meaning, and *mizthu-hu* (I separated it), *fa-nmaza* and *amtaza*, and *mayyiztuhu* (I distinguished it), *fa-tamayyaza*. That is, it is said to them this at the time of standing for questioning, when the people of the Garden are commanded to the Garden: "Get out from among them." Qatadah said: "They are removed from every good." Al-Dahhak said: "The criminals separate from one another: the Jews form one group, the Christians a group, the Magians a group, the Sabians a group, and the idol-worshippers a group." And he also said: "For each group in the Fire is a house they enter, and its door is closed, and they become *abdal* (replacements) that are seen." Dawud ibn al-Jarrah said: "The Muslims separate from the criminals, except the people of desires (*ahl al-ahwa'*), who remain with the criminals."

Then Allah, Majestic and Mighty, says to them: "Peace be upon My servants who obeyed Me and guarded My covenant in the unseen. I have chosen you, I have selected you, and I have preferred you. Go and enter the Garden without reckoning," and ﴿there is no fear upon you today, nor will you grieve﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 68]. (They pass over the Sirat like a flashing lightning, and its gates are opened for them.) Then the creation will be held in place at the gathering, and some will say to others: "O people, where is so-and-so and so-and-so?" At that time, some will be asking others, and a caller will call out: "Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in joy, reclining."

*Shughulin* and *shughlun* are two readings recited with both forms, like *ar-ru'ub* and *ar-ru'b*, and *as-suht* and *as-suht*, and this has been discussed before. [[See vol. 6, p. 184 of the printed edition.]]

*Fakihun*: al-Hasan said: "Joyful." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Happy." Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: "Admiring." Al-Suddi said: "Enjoying ease." The meanings are close. *Al-fukahah* is jesting and good speech. Abu Ja'far, Shaybah and al-A'raj read *fakihun* without an alif, and both are two dialects, like *al-farih* and *al-farih*, and *al-hadhir* and *al-hadhir*, as al-Farra' said. Al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubaydah said: *al-fakih* means one who possesses fruit, like *shahim* (fat-possessor), *lahim* (meat-possessor), *tamir* (date-possessor) and *labin* (milk-possessor), while *al-fakih* (in the sense of *al-mutafakkih*) means one who enjoys and one who lives in luxury. *Fakihun* without an alif, according to Qatadah, means "admiring." Abu Zayd said: "One says a man is *fakih* when he is good-natured and laughing."

Talhah ibn Musarrif read *fakihin* in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*).

﴿They and their spouses, in shades, upon couches, reclining﴾: *hum* is the subject and its predicate follows. It is permissible that *hum* be an emphatic pronoun, *wa-azwajuhum* be a conjunction upon the implied pronoun, and *muttaki'un* be an adjective of *fakihun*. The common reading is *fi zilalin* with a kasra on the *za'* and an alif. Ibn Mas'ud, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, al-A'mash, Yahya, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *fi zulalin* with a damma on the *za'* and without an alif. So *zilal* is the plural of *zill*, and *zulal* is the plural of *zullah*.

*'Ala al-arai'k*: this means the thrones in the canopied chambers. Its singular is *arikah*, like *safinah* and *safa'in*. The poet said:

"As if the redness of the rose upon its branches,
at the time of forenoon, in the garden of the one who laughs,
Are the cheeks of virgins who have blushed from shyness,
swaying with basil above the couches."

It is reported in a tradition from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whenever the people of the Garden have intercourse with their women, they return to being virgins." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Indeed, a man of the people of the Garden embraces the *hawra'* (a dark-eyed maiden) for seventy years, he does not tire of her and she does not tire of him. Whenever he comes to her, he finds her a virgin, and whenever he returns to her, his desire returns to him. He has intercourse with her with the strength of seventy men, and there is no emission between them. It comes without emission from him or from her."

﴿For them therein is fruit﴾: this is an inceptive clause with its predicate. ﴿And for them is whatever they call for﴾: the second *dal* in *yadda'una* is substituted from a *ta'*, because it is *yaftaʻilun* from *da'a*, meaning whoever asks for something is given it. This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah. So the meaning of *yadda'un* is "they wish," derived from *al-du'a'* (calling/asking). It was also said: the meaning is that whoever among them claims something, it is his, because Allah, Exalted is He, has disposed them so that none of them claims anything except what is fitting and good to claim. Yahya ibn Sallam said: *yadda'un* means "they desire." Ibn 'Abbas said: "They ask." The meanings are close.

Ibn al-Anbari said: "*Wa-lahum ma yadda'un*" is a good place to pause, and then you begin with *salam*, meaning: for them is peace. It is also permissible to make *salam* nominative, meaning: "and for them is whatever they call for, sealed/pure." On this view, it is not good to pause at *ma yadda'un*.

Al-Zajjaj said: *salam* is nominative as a substitute for *ma*, meaning: "and for them is that Allah sends peace upon them," and this is the wish of the people of the Garden. It is related from the hadith of Jarir ibn 'Abdullah al-Bajali that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "While the people of the Garden are in their bliss, a light shines upon them. They raise their heads, and behold, the Lord, Exalted is He, has looked down upon them from above, and He says: 'Peace be upon you, O people of the Garden.' That is His saying: '*Peace*, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful.' He looks at them, and they look at Him. They do not turn to anything of the bliss as long as they are looking at Him, until He veils Himself from them, and His light and blessings remain upon them in their homes." This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi and al-Qushayri. Its meaning is established in Sahih Muslim, and we have explained it in *Yunus* [[See vol. 8, p. 230 of the first printing]] at His saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best reward and more﴾ [Yunus: 26].

It is also permissible that *ma* be indefinite and *salam* an adjective of it, meaning: "and for them is whatever they call for, sealed." It is also permissible that *ma* be nominative by the inceptive, and *salam* the predicate of it. On these aspects, one does not pause at *wa-lahum ma yadda'un*.

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, *salaman* is a verbal noun (*masdar*), and if you wish, it can be in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning: "and for them is whatever they call for, with peace, or safety, or as something sealed." On this view, it is not good to pause at *yadda'un*.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi read *silm* as a new sentence, as if he said: "That is peace for them, they do not dispute about it." Then *wa-lahum ma yadda'un* is a complete sentence. It is also permissible that *salam* be a substitute for His saying *wa-lahum ma yadda'un*, and the predicate of *ma yadda'un* is *lahum*. It is also permissible that *salam* be another predicate, and the meaning of the statement is that it is theirs purely, without anyone disputing it.

*Qawlan* is a verbal noun, meaning: Allah says that, a saying; or He says it as a saying. The verb is omitted and its verbal noun indicates it. It is also permissible that the meaning be "and for them is whatever they call for, as a saying," that is, a promise from Allah. On this second view, it is not good to pause at *yadda'un*.

Al-Sijistani said: the pause at His saying *salam* is complete. This is an error, because *al-qawl* (the saying) is separate from what precedes it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And withdraw today, O criminals.﴾ It is said: *tamayyazu*, *amazu* and *amtazu* have the same meaning, and *mizthu-hu* (I separated it), *fa-nmaza* and *amtaza*, and *mayyiztuhu* (I distinguished it), *fa-tamayyaza*. That is, it is said to them this at the time of standing for questioning, when the people of the Garden are commanded to the Garden: "Get out from among them." Qatadah said: "They are removed from every good." Al-Dahhak said: "The criminals separate from one another: the Jews form one group, the Christians a group, the Magians a group, the Sabians a group, and the idol-worshippers a group." And he also said: "For each group in the Fire is a house they enter, and its door is closed, and they become *abdal* (replacements) that are seen." Dawud ibn al-Jarrah said: "The Muslims separate from the criminals, except the people of desires (*ahl al-ahwa'*), who remain with the criminals."

**Verse 60–64**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan?﴾ Here *al-'ahd* (covenant, charge) means *al-wasiyyah* (command or instruction). That is, "Did I not command you and convey to you through the tongues of the messengers?" "That you should not worship Satan" means that you should not obey him in disobeying Me. Al-Kisa'i said: the *la* is a prohibition (*nahy*). "And that you should worship Me": "and that you should worship Me" with the *nun* kasra, as the original form. Whoever pronounces it with a damma disliked a kasra followed by a damma. ﴿This is a straight path﴾, that is, worshipping Me is the upright religion.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he had certainly led astray from you∎﴾, that is, misled (*aghwa*). "A great multitude" (*jibillan kathiran*), that is, a great number of creatures, as Mujahid said. Qatadah said: great hosts. Al-Kalbi said: many nations. The meaning is one. The people of Madinah and 'Asim read *jibillan* with a kasra on the *jim* and the *ba'*. Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read *jubulan* with a damma on the *jim* and a sukun on the *ba'*. The rest read *jiblan*, with a damma on the *jim* and the *ba'* and a light *lam*. Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ubayd and al-Nadr ibn Anas read the *lam* with a shaddah. Abu Yahya and al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli read *jiblan*, with a kasra on the *jim*, a sukun on the *ba'* and a light *lam*. These are five readings (*qira'at*, recognized variant recitations). Al-Mahdawi and al-Tha'labi said: all of them are dialect forms (*lughat*) with the meaning "creation." Al-Nahhas said: the clearest of them is the first reading, and the evidence for this is that they unanimously read ﴿and the earlier generations (*al-jibillata al-awwalin*)﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 184], so *jibillan* is the plural of *jibillah*, and its derivation throughout is one. It is from *jabala Allah 'azza wa jall al-khalq*, meaning God created the creation, that is, He created them.

A sixth reading has also been mentioned: "*wa-laqad adalla minkum jilan kathiran*" with a *ya'*. It is reported from al-Dahhak that a single *jil* is ten thousand, and that *kathir* is what no one can count except God, Mighty and Majestic. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

﴿Did you not then use reason?﴾, that is, recognize his enmity and know that obedience to God is obligatory.

﴿This is Hell﴾, that is, the keepers of Hell will say to them: this is Hell which you were promised and which you denied.

It is related from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, God will gather the humans, the jinn, the earlier and the later generations in one plain. Then a neck of Fire will rise above the creatures and encompass them. Then a caller will call out: 'This is Hell which you were promised; burn in it today for what you used to disbelieve.' At that time the nations will fall to their knees, every nursing mother will be distracted from what she nursed, every pregnant woman will lay down her burden, and you will see people drunk, though they are not drunk, but the punishment of God is severe."

**Allah's words:** ﴿Today We shall seal their mouths, and their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will bear witness to what they used to earn﴾. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Anas ibn Malik, who said: We were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when he laughed and said: "Do you know what I am laughing at?" We said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "At the servant's address to his Lord, when he says: 'O Lord, did You not protect me from wrongdoing?' He says: 'Yes.' Then he says: 'I do not allow any witness against myself except from myself.' He says: 'Sufficient is yourself as a witness against you today, and the noble scribes as witnesses.' Then his mouth is sealed, and it is said to his limbs: 'Speak.' So they speak of his deeds. Then he is left free to speak, and he says: 'Away with you, and destruction! It was for your sake that I was contending.'" He also narrated it from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, in which it says: "Then it is said to him: 'Now We shall send forth Our witness against you.' He reflects within himself: 'Who is it that will bear witness against me?' Then his mouth is sealed, and it is said to his thigh ([[the addition from Sahih Muslim]]: and his flesh and his bones): 'Speak.' So his thigh, his flesh and his bones speak of his deeds. This is so that he may be left without excuse from himself. That is the hypocrite, and that is the one with whom Allah is angry."

At-Tirmidhi related from Mu'awiyah ibn Haydah, from the Prophet ﷺ, in a hadith he mentioned, that he pointed with his hand towards Syria and said: "From here to here you will be gathered, riding and on foot, and on the Day of Resurrection you will be dragged upon your faces, with a fidam (strainer) upon your mouths. You will be the seventy nations, you being the best of them and the most honoured by Allah. The first part of any one of you to speak (yu'rib, i.e., to express himself) will be his thigh." In another narration: "his thigh and his palm." The fidam is the strainer of the jug and the ewer. Al-Layth said so. Abu Ubayd said: It means that they are prevented from speaking until their thighs speak, and this is likened to the fidam placed on the ewer.

Then there are four views regarding the reason for the sealing. The first: because they said ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23], so Allah sealed their mouths until their limbs spoke. This was said by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari. The second: so that the people of the place of standing may recognise them and distinguish them from others. This was said by Ibn Ziyad.
