You will be the seventy nations, you being the best of them and the most honoured by Allah. The first part of any one of you to speak (yu'rib, i.e., to express himself) will be his thigh." In another narration: "his thigh and his palm." The fidam is the strainer of the jug and the ewer. Al-Layth said so. Abu Ubayd said: It means that they are prevented from speaking until their thighs speak, and this is likened to the fidam placed on the ewer.

Then there are four views regarding the reason for the sealing. The first: because they said ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23], so Allah sealed their mouths until their limbs spoke. This was said by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari. The second: so that the people of the place of standing may recognise them and distinguish them from others. This was said by Ibn Ziyad. The third: because the confession of one who does not speak is more forceful as proof than the confession of one who speaks, since it comes in the manner of a miracle, if it is a day that does not need a miracle. The fourth: so that he may know that his limbs, which were helpers for him in respect of his own self, have become witnesses against him in respect of his Lord.

If it is asked: Why did He say ﴿and their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will bear witness﴾, making what came from the hand "speech" and what came from the foot "testimony"? It is said: The hand is directly engaged in his action, while the foot is present, and the word of one who is present about another is testimony, while the word of the doer about himself is a confession of what he said or did. Therefore He expressed what proceeded from the hands by "speech" and what proceeded from the feet by "testimony."

It has also been narrated from Uqbah ibn Amir, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "The first bone of a human being to speak on the day when the mouths are sealed is his thigh, from the left leg." Al-Mawardi and al-Mahdawi mentioned it. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said: "I think that the first part of him to speak is his right thigh." Al-Mahdawi also mentioned it. Al-Mawardi said: It is possible that the thigh precedes the other limbs in speech because the pleasure of his sins is perceived by his senses which are in the lower half of it, the thigh; so it was fitting, because of its nearness to them, that it should precede in testifying about them. He said: And the left (thigh) preceded, because desire is stronger in the right parts of the limbs than in the left, so the left preceded the right because its desire is weaker. I say: or the reverse, because of the dominance of desire; or both together; and the palm, for the sum of all this is the completion of desire and pleasure. And Allah knows best.

**Allah's words:** ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes, so they would race for the path, but how could they see?﴾ Al-Kisa'i related: the verb ṭamasa has two forms, yaṭmisu and yaṭmusu. Among the lexicographers, al-maṭmus and aṭ-ṭamis mean the blind person who has no slit between his eyes. Ibn Abbas said: the meaning is: We would have blinded them to guidance, so they would never be guided to the path of truth. Al-Hasan and as-Suddi said: the meaning is: We would have left them blind, wandering about. So the meaning is: We would have blinded them, so they would not see a way to move about in their dwellings or elsewhere. This is the view chosen by at-Tabari. As for His words ﴿so they would race for the path﴾, that is, they would race for the road in order to pass through it. ﴿But how could they see?﴾ means: from where could they see?

Ata, Muqatil and Qatadah said, and it was also narrated from Ibn Abbas: "And if We willed, We would have gouged out the eyes of their misguidance, and blinded them to their error, and turned their sight from misguidance to guidance, so they would be guided and see their right course, and hasten towards the path of the Hereafter." Then He said: ﴿but how could they see?﴾, and We did not do that to them. That is, how would they be guided when the eye of guidance is obliterated, and they remain in misguidance?

It has also been narrated from Abdullah ibn Salam, concerning the interpretation of this verse, something other than what has preceded, and he interpreted it as referring to the Day of Resurrection. He said: When it is the Day of Resurrection and the Sirat is stretched out, a herald calls: "Let Muhammad ﷺ and his community stand up!" They stand up, the righteous and the wicked among them, following him so that they may cross the Sirat. When they are upon it, Allah obliterates the eyes of their wicked ones, so they race along the Sirat, but how could they see it until they pass it? Then a herald calls: "Let Jesus and his community stand up!" He stands, and the righteous and the wicked among them follow him, and their path is that path. The same applies to all the prophets, peace be upon them. An-Nahhas mentioned it. We have written it in at-Tadhkirah in its meaning, according to what Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned in his ar-Raqa'iq. Al-Qushayri also mentioned it.

Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: al-Aswad ibn al-Aswad took a stone, together with a group of the Banu Makhzum, to throw it at the Prophet ﷺ. Allah obliterated his sight, and the stone stuck to his hand, so he neither saw nor was guided, and the verse was revealed concerning him. The maṭmus is the one who has no slit between his eyelids, derived from "the wind obliterated the trace" (ṭamasa ar-rīḥ al-athar). This was said by al-Akhfash and al-Qutabi.

**Allah's words:** ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places, so they would not be able to proceed, nor could they return﴾. Al-Maskh is the alteration of the creation and its transformation into a stone, an inanimate object, or a beast. Al-Hasan said: That is, We would have made them sit, so they could neither go forward before them, nor turn back behind them. Likewise, an inanimate object neither advances nor retreats. Maskh may also be the changing of a human form into that of an animal; then that animal does not understand a place to aim for, so it is bewildered, neither advancing nor retreating. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the meaning is: If We willed, We would have destroyed them in their dwellings. It was also said: the meaning is: If We willed, We would have transformed them in the place where they dared to commit disobedience. Ibn Salam said: all of this is on the Day of Resurrection, when Allah obliterates their eyes on the Sirat.

Al-Hasan, as-Sulami, Zirr ibn Hubaysh, and Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr read "makanatihim" in the plural; the rest read it in the singular. Abu Haywah read "famā istaṭā'ū muḍiyyan" with a fatḥah on the mīm. Al-Muḍiyy with a ḍammah on the mīm is the verbal noun of yamḍī, "mudiyyan," meaning to go away.

**Allah's words:** ﴿And whoever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation﴾. Asim and Hamzah read "nunakkisuhu" with a ḍammah on the first nūn and a shaddah on the kāf, from at-tankīs (reversal). The rest read "nankusuhu" with a fatḥah on the first nūn and a ḍammah on the kāf, from nakastu ash-shay' ankusuhu nakṣan, meaning I turned the thing upon its head so it was overturned. Qatadah said: the meaning is that he returns to the state of decrepitude which resembles the state of childhood. Sufyan, concerning His words ﴿And whoever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation﴾, said: when he reaches eighty years, his body changes and his strength weakens. The poet said:

*Whoever lives long, the days have worn away his freshness,*
*and his two trusted companions, hearing and sight, have betrayed him.*

Thus long life turns youth into old age, strength into weakness, and increase into decrease, and this is the general case. The Prophet ﷺ sought refuge from being returned to the most abject age. Its explanation has been given in an-Nahl. [[See vol. 10, p. 140 onward, of the first or second edition.]] ﴿Will they not then understand?﴾ That whoever has done this to you is capable of resurrecting you. Nafi' and Ibn Dhakwan read "ta'qilūn" with the letter tā' (you). The rest read it with yā' (they).

**First:** Allah, the Exalted, informs about the condition of His Prophet (ﷺ) and rejects the claim of those among the disbelievers who said that he is a poet and that the Qur'an is poetry, by His saying: "We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him." Likewise, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not compose poetry and did not metrically arrange it. When he tried to recite an ancient verse by way of quotation, he would break its meter, and he would only convey its meanings. Among examples of this, he once recited the saying of Tarafa:

*"The days will reveal to you what you did not know,*
*And there will come to you one whom you did not provide with news."*

On another occasion, when he was asked who the best poet was, he recited the line:

*"Do you not see me, whenever I come to a visitor's camp,*
*I find in it [a host], even if it is not a good one?"*

He also once recited:

*"Would you make my plunder and the plunder of the slaves*
*Between al-Aqra' and ʿUyayna?"*

The Prophet (ﷺ) sometimes recited a correct verse, rarely. It was narrated that he recited the verse of ʿAbdullah ibn Rawaha:

*"A house that keeps his side away from its bed,*
*And when the beds become heavy with the polytheists."*

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: The Prophet (ﷺ) recited:

*"Islam and grey hair suffice a man as a restrainer."*

Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "O Messenger of Allah, the poet said:

*'Hurayra, leave off, if you prepare to depart,*
*And grey hair and Islam suffice a man as a restrainer.'"*

Then Abu Bakr or ʿUmar said: "I bear witness that you are the Messenger of Allah. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: 'We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him.'"

Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad narrated: "Poetry was more beloved to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) than much speech, but it was not possible for him."

**Second:** That he sometimes hit the meter does not necessitate that he knew poetry. Likewise, what occasionally comes in his prose that falls into a meter, such as his saying on the day of Hunayn and other occasions:

*"Are you not but a finger that was bled,*
*And in the way of Allah you suffered what you suffered?"*

And his saying:

*"I am the Prophet, there is no lie,*
*I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muttalib."*

Such things may occur in the verses of the Qur'an and in all speech, and that is not poetry nor of its nature. Examples are His saying: "You will not attain righteousness until you spend from what you love" (Q. 3:92), His saying: "Help from Allah and a near victory" (Q. 61:13), and His saying: "And bowls like water troughs and firmly rooted cooking pots" (Q. 34:13), and other verses. Ibn al-ʿArabi mentioned some of these verses, discussed them, and removed them from the meter.

However, Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash said regarding the saying "I am the Prophet, there is no lie" that it is not poetry. Al-Khalil said in *Kitab al-ʿAyn* that what comes as *sajʿ* (rhymed prose) in two halves is not poetry. It was also narrated from him that it is from *manhuk al-rajaz* (a truncated form of *rajaz* meter). It has been said that it cannot be from *manhuk al-rajaz* except by pausing on the *bāʾ* in his saying "lā kadhib" and in his saying "ʿabd al-Muttalib." He did not know how the Prophet (ﷺ) said it. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: "The most apparent state is that he said 'lā kadhibu,' with the *bāʾ* raised, and the *bāʾ* of 'ʿabd al-Muttalib' is in the genitive by idafa (construction)."

Al-Nahhas said: Some said: "The transmission is only with the *iʿrab* (grammatical inflection). If it is with *iʿrab*, it is not poetry, because if one opens, raises, or nunates the *bāʾ* of the first line, and kasrs the *bāʾ* of the second line, it leaves the meter of poetry." Some said: "This meter is not from poetry." Ibn al-ʿArabi said: "This is an obstinacy against clear evidence, because the poetry of the Arabs on this pattern has been transmitted by al-Khalil and others."

As for his saying "Are you not but a finger that was bled," it was said that it is from the *bahr al-sarīʿ* (the sarīʿ meter), and that is only the case if the *tāʾ* in *dumiyat* is kasred. If it is vowelled with a sukun, it cannot be poetry at all, because these two words in this form become *faʿūl*, and *faʿūl* has no place in the *bahr al-sarīʿ*. Perhaps the Prophet (ﷺ) said it with the *tāʾ* sukun, or with the *tāʾ* vowelled without prolongation. The reliable position on the question, granting that this is poetry, is that the objection falls away. It also does not follow that the Prophet (ﷺ), who was not knowledgeable of poetry nor a poet, quoting a scant verse or hitting the two rhyming endings in *rajaz* or other meters, necessitates that its speaker be knowledgeable of poetry. He is not called a poet by scholarly consensus, just as one who sews a thread is not a tailor.

Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of "We did not teach him poetry" is: We did not teach him that he would versify; that is, We did not make him a poet. This does not prevent him from reciting some poetry. Al-Nahhas said: This is among the best of what has been said on this.

It has also been said that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, only informed that He did not teach him poetry, and did not state that he would not recite poetry; this is the apparent meaning of the statement. Another clear position was stated, whose proponent claimed it to be a consensus of the linguists: they said, "Whoever utters a metrical speech without intending it as poetry is not a poet, he has only coincided with poetry." This is a clear position. They said: What Allah negated of His Prophet (ﷺ) is the knowledge of poetry and its types, its *ʿarūḍ* (prosodic patterns) and its rhymes, and being characterized by composing it. He was not described as such by consensus. Do you not see that the Quraysh consulted among themselves about what they would say to the Arabs regarding him when they came to them during the season (of pilgrimage)? Some of them said: "We will say he is a poet." The discerning among them said: "By Allah, the Arabs will surely call you a liar, for they know the types of poetry, and by Allah his speech does not resemble any of them, nor is his speech poetry." Unays, the brother of Abu Dharr, said: "I have weighed his speech against the categories of poetry" and it did not fit that it was poetry. This was narrated by Muslim, and Unays was among the most eloquent of the Arab poets. Likewise Utba ibn Abi Rabiʿa, when he spoke with him, said: "By Allah, it is neither poetry, nor soothsaying, nor sorcery," as will be explained in his account in the surah of *Fussilat*, Allah willing. Likewise others among the eloquent Arabs of pure lineage and the eloquent tongues said. Moreover, what flows on the tongue of metrical speech is not counted as poetry; only that which follows the meter of poetry with intention is counted from it. A speaker may say, "Our shaykh narrated to us," and he calls out, "O companion of al-Kisāʾī," and this is not counted as poetry. A man in his illness, who was among the common sane people, called out: "Take me to the physician and say he has been cauterized."

**Third:** Ibn al-Qasim narrated from Malik that he was asked about reciting poetry, and he said: "Do not do it much, for among its faults is that Allah says: 'We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him.'" He said: "It has reached me that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) wrote to Abu Musa al-Ashʿari: 'Gather the poets before you, ask them about poetry, and whether any knowledge of it remains with them, and bring Labid to me.'" He said: "So he gathered them and questioned them. They said: 'We know it and compose it.' He asked Labid, and he said: 'I have not composed poetry since I heard Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, say: "Alif Lam Mim. This is the Book, in which there is no doubt" (Q. 2:1–2).'" Ibn al-ʿArabi said: "This verse is not among the faults of poetry, just as His saying: 'You did not recite before it any Book, nor did you write it with your right hand' (Q. 29:48) is not among the faults of writing. Since illiteracy is not a fault of handwriting, likewise the negation of versification from the Prophet (ﷺ) is not a fault of poetry."

It was narrated that al-Maʾmun said to Abu ʿAli al-Minqari: "It has reached me that you are illiterate, that you do not compose poetry correctly, and that you commit errors in speech." He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, as for error in speech, my tongue has sometimes slipped in something. As for illiteracy and breaking poetic meter, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not write and did not compose poetry correctly." He said to him: "I asked you about three faults in you, and you added a fourth, which is ignorance. O ignorant one! That was a virtue for the Prophet (ﷺ), but in you and those like you it is a deficiency. The Prophet (ﷺ) was prevented from that only to negate suspicion about him, not because of a defect in poetry or writing."

**Fourth:** His saying, "nor is it befitting for him," means: nor is it befitting for him to compose it. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, made this one of the signs of His Prophet (ﷺ), so that doubt would not enter the minds of those to whom he was sent, that they might think he was powerful in the Qur'an because of a natural capacity for poetry. No heretic has a valid objection on this basis, by way of the meter that occurs in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Messenger, because what coincides with the meter of poetry without intending it as poetry is not poetry. Had it been poetry, then everyone among the common people who utters something metrical without knowing meter would be a poet, as has been explained earlier.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of "nor is it befitting for him" is: the composing of poetry is not easy for him, except by invention. "It is only" — that is, this which he recites to you — "a reminder and a clear Qur'an." His saying: "That it may warn him who is alive" — that is, whose heart is alive, said Qatada. Al-Dahhak said: "Sensible." It was also said: The meaning is that it may warn him who is a believer in Allah's knowledge. This is according to the reading with the *tāʾ*, addressing the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is the reading of Nafiʿ and Ibn ʿAmir. The rest read with the *yāʾ*, meaning "that Allah may warn," or "that Muhammad (ﷺ) may warn," or "that the Qur'an may warn." It was narrated from Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ "li-yunḏar" with a *fatḥa* on the *yāʾ* and the *dhāl*. "And that the word may be due against the disbelievers": that is, that the proof may be established against the disbelievers through the Qur'an.

No heretic has a valid objection on this basis, by way of the meter that occurs in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Messenger, because what coincides with the meter of poetry without intending it as poetry is not poetry. Had it been poetry, then everyone among the common people who utters something metrical without knowing meter would be a poet, as has been explained earlier.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of "nor is it befitting for him" is: the composing of poetry is not easy for him, except by invention. "It is only" — that is, this which he recites to you — "a reminder and a clear Qur'an." His saying: "That it may warn him who is alive" — that is, whose heart is alive, said Qatada. Al-Dahhak said: "Sensible." It was also said: The meaning is that it may warn him who is a believer in Allah's knowledge. This is according to the reading with the *tāʾ*, addressing the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is the reading of Nafiʿ and Ibn ʿAmir. The rest read with the *yāʾ*, meaning "that Allah may warn," or "that Muhammad (ﷺ) may warn," or "that the Qur'an may warn." It was narrated from Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ "li-yunḏar" with a *fatḥa* on the *yāʾ* and the *dhāl*. "And that the word may be due against the disbelievers": that is, that the proof may be established against the disbelievers through the Qur'an.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 71–73:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they not see that We have created for them﴾. This is the seeing of the heart, meaning: do they not look, take heed, and reflect? "Of what Our hands have made" means: of what We originated and made without intermediary, agency, or partnership. "Mā" here means "that which" (alladhī), and the returning pronoun (hā') has been omitted because of the length of the noun phrase. If you make "mā" a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah), you do not need to supply the pronoun. "Cattle" (an'āman) is the plural of ni'am, and ni'am is masculine. ﴿So they are owners of them﴾, meaning: controllers, dominant over them. "And We have made them subservient to them", meaning: We made them subject to them, so that a child leads the great camel, strikes it, and turns it however he wishes, without it leaving his obedience. ﴿From them is their means of riding﴾. The recitation of the common readers is with a fatḥah on the rā' (rakūbuhum), meaning "their ridden beast (markūbuhum)," as one says "ḥalūb" for "maḥlūb" (a milked [she-camel]). Al-A'mash, al-Ḥasan, and Ibn al-Sumayqa read "fa-minhā rukūbuhum" with a ḍammah on the rā', as a verbal noun. It is narrated from ʿĀ'ishah that she recited "fa-minhā rakūbatuhum," and likewise in her muṣḥaf. "Rakūb" and "rakūbah" are the same, like "ḥalūb" and "ḥalūbah," and "ḥamūl" and "ḥamūlah." The Kufan grammarians report that the Arabs say: "imra'ah ṣabūr and shakūr" without the hā', and they say: "shāh ḥalūbah" and "nāqah rakūbah," because they wanted to distinguish between that to which the action belongs and that upon which the action falls. So they omit the hā' from what is the doer and affirm it in what is the object. As the poet said [[It is ʿAntarah ibn Shaddād.]]:

"In it are forty-two milch camels (ḥalūbah), and black ones like the darkest feather of the glossy raven."

Accordingly, on this view it should be rakūbatahum. As for the Basrans, they say the hā' was omitted by way of nisbah (attribution). The proof for the first opinion is what al-Jarmi narrated from Abu ʿUbaydah, who said: "rakūbah" can apply to the singular and the plural, while "rakūb" applies only to the plural. On this basis it is a masculine form for a plural. Abu Ḥātim claimed that "fa-minhā rukūbuhum" with a ḍammah on the rā' is not permissible, because it is a verbal noun, and "rukūb" is what is ridden. Al-Farrā' permitted "fa-minhā rukūbuhum" with a ḍammah on the rā', just as one says "fa-minhā ukulahum" and "fa-minhā shurbuhum." ﴿And from them they eat﴾, from their meat. ﴿And for them in them are benefits﴾, from their wool, their fur, their hair, their fats, their flesh, and other things. ﴿And drinks﴾, meaning their milk. Both (manāfiʿ and mashārib) are not diptote, because they are among the plurals that have no counterpart in the singular. ﴿Will they not then be thankful?﴾ to God for His blessings.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 74–76:

What they conceal and what they reveal. [Allah's] statement: ﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah, hoping they might be helped﴾. That is: they have seen these signs from Our power, and then they have taken gods besides Us which have no ability to act. "Hoping they might be helped" means: because of what they hope for from their help for them, should a punishment descend upon them. Among the Arabs there are those who say: la'allahu an yaf'ala (perhaps he will do). "They are unable to help them": meaning the gods. They are referred to with the plural suffix of the sound masculine plural (wa-n), because He has described them with the description of human beings. "And they" meaning the disbelievers "for them" that is, for the gods, "are a host brought forward" (jundun muhdarun). Al-Hasan said: they defend them and ward off [harm] from them. Qatadah said: that is, they become angry on their behalf in the world. It was also said: the meaning is that they worship the gods and serve them, so they are to them like a host, while the gods are unable to help them. These three statements are close in meaning. It was also said: the gods are a host for the worshippers, brought forward with them in the Fire, so that some of them do not ward off others. It was also said: the meaning is that these idols are, for these disbelievers, a host of Allah against them in Hell, because they curse them and disown their worship. It was also said: the gods are a host for them, brought forward on the Day of Resurrection to aid them in their assumptions. And in a report: it is said that for every people will be represented what they used to worship in the world besides Allah, and they will follow it into the Fire; so they have a host brought forward. I say: the meaning of this report is what is established in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of Abu Hurairah, and in al-Tirmidhi from him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah will gather the people on the Day of Resurrection in one level plain. Then the Lord of the worlds will look down upon them and say: 'Let every person follow what he used to worship.' So for the owner of the cross, his cross will be represented, for the owner of the images, his images, and for the owner of the fire, his fire; and they will follow what they used to worship, and the Muslims will remain." And he mentioned the hadith in full.

﴿So let not their saying grieve you﴾. This is the eloquent reading. Among the Arabs there are those who say yahzunuka. The purpose is consolation for His Prophet, peace be upon him, meaning: let not their saying, "a poet, a sorcerer," grieve you. Then the speech is complete, and He resumes, saying: ﴿Indeed, We know what they conceal and what they reveal﴾, of speech and action, and what they display; so We will recompense them for that.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 77:

Clear (mubin). His statement, the Exalted: ﴿Does not man see that We created him from a drop of semen?﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-insan" (the man) is 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he is al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi. Al-Hasan said: he is Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi.

Ibn Ishaq said the same, and Ibn Wahb narrated it from Malik. ﴿That We created him from a drop (nutfah)﴾, and nutfah is the small amount of water, from "nataffa" meaning it dripped. ﴿Then behold, he is an open adversary (khasim mubin)﴾, that is, one who argues in disputation and makes his proof clear. He means by this that he became, after having been "nothing worth mentioning," an open adversary. The reason is that he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a decayed bone and said: "O Muhammad, do you think that Allah will bring this back to life after it has crumbled to dust?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Yes, and Allah will resurrect you and cast you into the Fire." Then this verse was revealed.

﴿And he presents a parable for Us and forgets his own creation. He says, "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?"﴾ On this verse there are two issues.

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿And he presents a parable for Us and forgets his own creation﴾, means: he forgets that We created him from a lifeless drop (*nutfah*) and then put life into him. His answer is ready within himself. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Yes, and Allah will resurrect you and cast you into the Fire." This is evidence for the validity of *qiyas* (analogical reasoning), because Allah, exalted and mighty is He, argued against those who denied the Resurrection by the first creation. ﴿He says, "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?"﴾ means: crumbling. It is said, "The bone decayed (*ramma*), so it is *rameem* and *rimam*." He said *rameem* and not *rameemah*, because it is an altered form (*ma'dulah*) from the pattern *fa'ilah*. Whatever is altered from its proper form and pattern is turned away from its grammatical inflection (*i'rab*), as in His saying, ﴿Your mother was not unchaste﴾ [Maryam: 28], where the *ha'* is dropped because the word has been turned away from *baghiyah*. It has been said that this disbeliever said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Tell me, if I crush it and scatter it in the wind, will Allah restore it?" Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Say, "He will give them life who brought them into being the first time."﴾ That is, from nothing. So He is able to restore it in the second creation from something, namely the coccyx (*ʿajb al-dhanab*). It is also said *ʿajb al-dhanab*, with the letter *yāʾ*. ﴿And He is Knowing of every creation﴾ means: how He originates it and restores it.

**The second issue:** This verse is evidence that there is life in bones, and that they become impure by death. This is the view of Abu Hanifa [[This contradicts the Hanafi school and what the author stated earlier in vol. 10, p. 155, that Abu Hanifa holds the bone of a dead animal to be pure.]] and some of al-Shafiʿi's companions. Al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him, said: there is no life in them. This was discussed earlier in Surat al-Nahl.

If it is said: by His saying, "Who will give life to bones," He means the owners of the bones, and placing the *mudaf* (the governing noun) in the position of the *mudaf ilayh* (the governed noun) is common in the language and found in the Shariah. We say: this is only acceptable when there is a necessity, and there is no necessity here that calls for this implied meaning. Nor does the sense require this supposition, since the Creator, glorified is He, has informed us of it, He is able to do it, and reality bears witness to it, for the sensation that is the sign of life is present in them. This was said by Ibn al-ʿArabi.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 80–83:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who has made for you fire from the green tree⁠—﴾ He, exalted is He, drew attention to His oneness and indicated the perfection of His power in bringing the dead to life, through what they witness of the bringing forth of the dry, burnt thing from the moist, green wood. This is because the disbeliever said: the sperm is hot and moist by the nature of life, so life comes out of it; and the bone is cold and dry by the nature of death, so how can life come out of it? So Allah, exalted is He, revealed: "Who has made for you fire from the green tree," meaning: the green tree contains water, and water is cold and moist, the opposite of fire, and the two do not come together. Yet Allah brought forth fire from it. So He is able to bring forth an opposite from an opposite, and He is capable of all things. It is said that the verse refers to what is in the markh (al-mirkh, a tree) and the 'affar (a shrub), which are the firestarters of the Arabs. From this is their saying: "In every tree there is fire," and "the markh and the 'affar have been given their due."[[Istamjada al-markh wal-'affar: meaning they have drawn much and taken from the fire what suffices them. It is a proverb used in preferring some thing over another.]] The 'affar is the upper firestick (zand), and the markh is the lower firestick (zandah).
